## Purpose {.unnumbered .unlisted}

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}
\begin{marginfigure}
\resizebox{0.92\linewidth}{!}{\mlphysicalstackfull{20}{20}{20}{20}{20}}
\end{marginfigure}
:::

_Why can a machine that completes every trial still lack the evidence to be allowed among people?_

A successful trial shows what a machine did under the conditions it happened to meet, while permission to operate is a claim about every condition it may meet next. Thousands of clean runs on a dry floor say nothing about the stop on a floor no trial touched, and a brake that stopped the machine last month may not stop it inside the same distance after its lining wears. A machine granted authority on demonstrations therefore carries untested premises into service, where the first test of each one is the event it was meant to prevent. Deciding to deploy requires stating which physical claims the evidence supports, under which conditions and for how long, refusing or narrowing operation wherever a premise remains unknown, and withdrawing the grant when brakes wear, sensors shift, or software changes. At the causal boundary, authority must expire when its physical justification does, because a later software correction cannot undo motion already produced.

{{< pagebreak >}}

::: {.callout-learning-objectives}

- Construct a claim-argument-evidence (CAE) safety case as an auditable engineering assertion DAG linking bounded operating envelopes to empirical hardware evidence
- Grade each claim's premises as measured, datasheet, illustrative, or unknown, and select the verdict (`UNCOND`, `COND`, or `REFUSE`) they support
- Join task-success, cycle-time, and intervention evidence to the physical measurements and restrictions supporting a conditional release
- Specify standing-condition cadences and validated responses separately from the execution leases that bound individual action chunks
- Diagnose unsupported warrants, hidden contextual assumptions, and compound defeaters through adversarial review of a release argument
- Design a cryptographically sealed release manifest that binds upstream engineering records by digest and fails closed on any mismatch
- Determine which claims a policy or software update reopens, and why shadow operation cannot substitute for closed-loop qualification

:::

## The Decision to Deploy {#sec-release-decision-to-deploy}

Every machine that works among people passes through a release decision, the point at which its builders grant it authority to operate outside the laboratory. In conventional software, release is a reversible step. A faulty build can be withdrawn, and the cost of the error is bounded by the time needed to revert it. For a physical machine the grant differs in kind. Each action the release permits delivers energy across the causal boundary, so an error in the release is discovered as a stop that ends too late or a contact that presses too hard, and no rollback recalls it. Industrial machinery, driverless vehicles, and aircraft have long met this problem with a documented argument, a safety case, that states what the machine is claimed to do, under which conditions, and on what evidence. Physical AI inherits that practice and adds a difficulty of its own. A learned policy cannot be argued safe from its structure, and trials alone cannot demonstrate the rare failures that matter most.

The central question of release is therefore which claims the evidence licenses, under which physical conditions, and for how long. This chapter treats the answer as a bounded, revocable engineering judgment rather than a score. The argument begins with a permitted operating envelope and links each physical claim to evidence. Its conclusion is full operation, restricted operation, or refusal, and standing conditions specify when that conclusion expires. A worked adjudication and an adversarial review test the argument, a signed manifest carries its decision into the running machine, and every later update must return through it.

The warehouse mobile manipulator shows why a record of success does not settle that question. It must drive past rack ends, open a spring-latched cage door, and hand a ceramic mug to a coworker. Each task requires a different physical claim: sufficient stopping clearance, bounded latch force, or bounded handover contact. A successful run shows that the machine completed those tasks under the conditions encountered. A release decision must establish which conditions it may encounter next and which evidence supports operation there.

Verification has specified how to stress the machine's timing, bus contention, and sensor-failure assumptions under injected faults (@sec-verification-hardware-fault-injection). Its illustrative records name predeclared oracles and untested gaps; they do not report completed physical trials. The systems engineering task therefore shifts from finding individual software bugs to formally bounding what the empirical evidence licenses. Neither offline validation accuracy (@sec-evaluation-closed-loop-dynamics) nor a run of clean demonstrations (@sec-verification-fault-injection) satisfies that requirement. Deciding to deploy is not a statistical prediction or an aggregate benchmark score; it is an auditable engineering adjudication of whether the physical evidence bounds the operational risk of the machine within a named operational design domain.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The empirical verification evidence backing release claims is produced in @sec-verification-hardware-fault-injection.
:::

A deployment must also deliver useful service inside the supported envelope. The closed-loop task evidence of @sec-evaluation-logs establishes whether the policy completes the intended work, how often intervention interrupts it, and which conditions defeat it. Those results must be evaluated under the speed, payload, and site restrictions the release case can support. A machine that can only stop safely has not demonstrated useful task capability; a capable policy has not thereby justified actuator authority. The deployment decision joins both arguments for the same task and operating conditions.

The release case is scoped to service at one site. The signed fault records of @sec-verification-fault-manifest contribute evidence about particular failures, while clearance surveys, loaded stopping trials, and contact measurements support the physical criteria. The engineer must connect each record to the claim it supports and retain every premise the record leaves open. Before any record can be connected, the claims themselves must be stated as physical criteria that the machine either satisfies or fails.

## The Deployment Authorization Criterion {#sec-release-question}

At a rack end, the base must stop inside the available clearance. During handover, the arm must stay within the assessed contact-force limit. Both claims depend on the response arriving before its deadline. These requirements give release authorization testable physical criteria:
$$d_{\text{stop}}(v, \tau_{\text{delay}}, a_{\text{brake}}, \delta_{\text{loc}}, \epsilon_{\text{track}}) \le D_{\text{clear}}, \quad F_{\text{contact}}(v, m_{\text{eff}}, k_h) \le F_{\text{limit}}, \quad T_{\text{exec}} \le T_{\text{deadline}}.$$

Each criterion is a physical inequality, so release authorization cannot rest on intuition, demonstrations, or aggregate benchmark scores. It requires an auditable argument that links each inequality to measured observation ages, worst-case execution time bounds, braking and contact trials, and a validated fallback. The inequalities also inherit the individual machine's calibration, its sensor transforms, joint offsets, and torque constants, so a lost or drifted calibration invalidates a stopping budget even when no software has changed.

For the warehouse mobile manipulator, the release question is whether evidence satisfies these criteria for each of its three tasks inside a scoped operating envelope. The release case names the assessed physical bounds, the specified hardware fault model, and the validated permission and fallback ladder. It can support a revocable grant of tracking authority while those physical conditions hold; it cannot infer protection against uncharacterized or unmodeled hazards from finite test runs (\ref{dfn-release-goal-structured-safety-case}).

::: {#dfn-release-goal-structured-safety-case .callout-definition title="Claim-argument-evidence safety case"}

***Claim-argument-evidence safety case***\index{Claim-argument-evidence safety case!definition}\index{Safety case!physical AI} is the auditable, structured assurance argument for a specified physical machine, operating envelope, hazard criteria, and fault model, linking top-level safety claims to concrete empirical evidence through explicit engineering warrants.

1.  **Significance**: Transforms subjective, informal deployment confidence into an auditable, machine-readable argument graph, a directed acyclic graph (DAG) that connects top-level physical invariance claims to concrete empirical evidence across the entire cyber-physical stack.
2.  **Distinction**: Unlike stateless software unit tests or static model validation scorecards, a physical safety case explicitly links operational design domain capability tokens, hardware fault-injection ledgers, sensor extrinsic calibration invariants, and deterministic runtime enforcer tripwires to argue, with stated confidence, that residual risk is acceptable for the named envelope.
3.  **Common pitfall**: Treating the safety case as a retrospective bureaucratic checklist completed after development, rather than an executable architectural contract that actively gates release manifests and runtime motor authority.

:::

```{python}
#| label: calc-release-contact-premises
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ CONTACT PREMISES INHERITED FROM THE ENFORCEMENT RECORD
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: every contact number this chapter quotes (@sec-release-question,
# │          @tbl-16-cae-scorecard, @sec-release-case-worked-full). The
# │          derivation is taught in @sec-enforcement-intentional-contact.
# │ Goal:    read the contact premises exactly as the enforcement chapter
# │          derives them, so release adjudicates and never re-derives.
# │ Show:    nothing directly; the release cells below read this class.
# │ How:     mirrors calc-enforcement-contact-force (EnforcementContactForce)
# │          line for line: same MLSysIM functions, same registry inputs, same
# │          guards. Chapters render in separate kernels, so the class is
# │          rebuilt here; the identical guards make any drift between the
# │          two chapters fail the build. Edit both cells together.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.physics.robotics import (
    calc_latch_contact_stopping_profile,
    calc_reduced_mass,
    calc_transient_impact_force,
    calc_transient_contact_speed_limit,
)
from mlsysim.fmt import check

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class EnforcementContactForce:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    v_latch = AISLE.v_latch_approach  # category: chosen (guarded approach)
    v_latch_high = AISLE.v_latch_high  # category: illustrative (policy's proposed approach)
    k_latch = AISLE.k_latch  # category: illustrative
    f_trip = AISLE.f_latch_tripwire  # category: illustrative
    t_contact = AISLE.t_contact_response  # category: illustrative (contact loop)
    f_lim = AISLE.f_latch_limit  # category: illustrative
    m_eff = RM.arm_effective_contact_mass  # category: derived
    m_hand = AISLE.m_contact_human  # category: datasheet (ISO/TS 15066 hand body model)
    k_hand = AISLE.k_contact_human  # category: datasheet (ISO/TS 15066 hand body model)
    f_contact = AISLE.f_contact_criterion  # category: chosen
    v_handover = AISLE.v_handover  # category: chosen (handover approach under accept_item)
    tcp_limit = RM.tcp_speed_limit  # category: chosen (free-space TCP limit)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    stop_lo = calc_latch_contact_stopping_profile(v_latch, scenario=AISLE)
    stop_hi = calc_latch_contact_stopping_profile(v_latch_high, scenario=AISLE)
    df_dt = stop_lo["df_dt"]
    f_cmd = stop_lo["f_at_brake_onset"]
    x_rem = stop_lo["x_remaining"]
    a_arm = stop_lo["a_arm_needed"]
    t_arm_stop = stop_lo["t_arm_stop"]
    f_cmd_hi = stop_hi["f_at_brake_onset"]
    a_arm_hi = stop_hi["a_arm_needed"]
    m_red = calc_reduced_mass(m_eff, m_hand).to(kilogram)
    f_at_tcp_limit = calc_transient_impact_force(tcp_limit, m_eff, k_hand, human_mass=m_hand).to(newton)
    f_ratio = (f_at_tcp_limit / f_contact).to("dimensionless").magnitude
    f_handover = calc_transient_impact_force(v_handover, m_eff, k_hand, human_mass=m_hand).to(newton)
    f_handover_clamped = calc_transient_impact_force(v_handover, m_eff, k_hand).to(newton)
    v_ceiling = calc_transient_contact_speed_limit(f_contact, m_eff, k_hand, human_mass=m_hand).to(meter / second)
    v_ceiling_clamped = calc_transient_contact_speed_limit(f_contact, m_eff, k_hand).to(meter / second)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (identical to calc-enforcement-contact-force) ─────────────
    check(abs(f_cmd.to(newton).magnitude - 39.0) < 1e-9, "Latch force at brake onset, guarded approach, is 39 N.")
    check(abs(x_rem.to(millimeter).magnitude - 0.1525) < 5e-5, "Remaining latch compression is 0.15 mm.")
    check(abs(a_arm.to(meter / second**2).magnitude - 2.95) < 5e-3, "The guarded stop needs about 3 m/s^2 (2.95).")
    check(abs(t_arm_stop.to(millisecond).magnitude - 10.0) < 0.5, "The guarded stop takes about 10 ms.")
    check(abs(f_cmd_hi.to(newton).magnitude - 95.0) < 1e-9, "Latch force at brake onset, unsupported approach, is 95 N.")
    check(abs(a_arm_hi.to(meter / second**2).magnitude - 400.0) < 1e-6, "The unsupported approach needs 400 m/s^2.")
    check(f_cmd < f_lim and f_cmd_hi < f_lim, "Both approaches reach brake onset below the latch limit.")
    check(abs(m_eff.to(kilogram).magnitude - 12.0) < 1e-9, "Arm effective contact mass is 12.0 kg.")
    check(abs(m_red.magnitude - 0.5714) < 5e-5, "Hand-arm reduced mass is 0.571 kg.")
    check(abs(f_at_tcp_limit.magnitude - 207.02) < 0.01, "Transient force at the TCP limit is 207 N.")
    check(abs(f_handover.magnitude - 20.70) < 0.01, "Transient handover force is 20.7 N.")
    check(abs(f_handover_clamped.magnitude - 94.87) < 0.01, "Clamped handover force is 94.9 N.")
    check(f_handover < f_contact < f_handover_clamped, "Transient passes and clamped fails the criterion.")
    check(abs(v_ceiling.magnitude - 0.2415) < 5e-5, "Free-hand ceiling is 0.24 m/s.")
    check(abs(v_ceiling_clamped.magnitude - 0.0527) < 5e-5, "Clamped-hand ceiling is 0.053 m/s.")
    check(v_ceiling_clamped < v_handover < v_ceiling, "The handover cap sits between the clamped and free-hand ceilings.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    # Raw quantities only; each release cell formats what it quotes.
```

```{python}
#| label: calc-release-operating-envelope
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ THE MACHINE'S OPERATING ENVELOPE FOR RELEASE
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-release-question (envelope and conditional-zone paragraphs),
# │          @tbl-16-odd-invariants, the contact-criteria paragraph after it, and
# │          the binding-contract paragraphs of @sec-release-three-verdicts, and
# │          the empirical-sufficiency probe of @sec-release-adversarial-review.
# │ Goal: Scope the release case to the running machine's operating envelope.
# │ Show: aisle speed and its ceiling, tote-rack payload, the friction bands and
# │       the inspected-floor ceiling, the clear distance, the latch and handover
# │       speeds with their limits, the slow-downs before a takeover, and the
# │       restricted speed on inspected floors.
# │ How: RM/AISLE fields; ceilings from calc_scurve_max_permitted_velocity (the
# │      jerk-limited S-curve stop; jerk bound = the reference C2 polynomial's
# │      peak jerk at the drive limit) and the three overheads; mu_min = a_brake/g.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, fmt_velocity, fmt_length, fmt_mass, fmt_force, fmt_latency, check
from mlsysim.physics.robotics import calc_c2_stop_suffix, calc_scurve_max_permitted_velocity

# ┌── 1. LOAD: the running machine and its site ─────────────────────────────────
RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator  # category: illustrative (running machine)
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle  # category: illustrative (aisle scene; speeds, lease, and tick chosen)
g_std = (1 * ureg.standard_gravity).to(meter / second**2)  # category: datasheet (standard gravity, a defined physical constant; Pint)
v_restricted = 1.0 * meter / second  # category: chosen (scenario assumption: restricted mode on inspected floors, the value @sec-frontier uses)

# ┌── 2. EXECUTE: ceilings and friction bands ───────────────────────────────────
# Jerk bound: the reference C2 polynomial's peak jerk at the drive limit (@sec-planning-c2-stopping-suffix)
j_brake = calc_c2_stop_suffix(RM.base.max_velocity, AISLE.a_brake)["peak_jerk"].to(meter / second**3)
overhead_loc = AISLE.delta_loc + AISLE.eps_track
v_ceiling = calc_scurve_max_permitted_velocity(AISLE.d_clear, AISLE.tau_delay, AISLE.a_brake, j_brake, overhead_loc, AISLE.delta_margin).to(
    meter / second
)
mu_min = (AISLE.a_brake / g_std).to("dimensionless").magnitude
# The floor caps the deceleration; the jerk bound belongs to the load and is unchanged.
a_inspected = min(AISLE.a_brake, (AISLE.mu_inspected_floor * g_std).to(meter / second**2))
v_inspected_ceiling = calc_scurve_max_permitted_velocity(AISLE.d_clear, AISLE.tau_delay, a_inspected, j_brake, overhead_loc, AISLE.delta_margin).to(
    meter / second
)
# Handover ceilings are enforcement premises (calc-release-contact-premises).
v_handover_ceiling = EnforcementContactForce.v_ceiling
v_handover_ceiling_clamped = EnforcementContactForce.v_ceiling_clamped

# ┌── 3. GUARD: canon values quoted in the prose and the table ──────────────────
check(abs(v_ceiling.magnitude - 1.4367) < 5e-5, "Unconditional aisle speed ceiling is 1.44 m/s")
check(AISLE.v_aisle < v_ceiling, "Chosen aisle speed sits under its ceiling")
check(abs(mu_min - 0.204) < 5e-4, "Friction floor is 0.204")
check(mu_min < AISLE.mu_dry, "Dry concrete exceeds the friction floor")
check(mu_min > AISLE.mu_inspected_floor, "Inspected floor requires speed restriction")
check(abs(v_inspected_ceiling.magnitude - 1.2309) < 5e-5, "Restricted ceiling on inspected floors is 1.23 m/s")
check(v_restricted < v_inspected_ceiling, "Chosen restricted mode sits under its ceiling")
check(abs(v_handover_ceiling.magnitude - 0.2415) < 5e-5, "Transient (free-hand) handover ceiling is 0.24 m/s")
check(AISLE.v_handover < v_handover_ceiling, "Chosen handover speed sits under its transient ceiling")
check(abs(v_handover_ceiling_clamped.magnitude - 0.0527) < 5e-5, "Clamped-hand handover ceiling is 0.053 m/s")
check(AISLE.v_handover > v_handover_ceiling_clamped, "Chosen handover speed exceeds the clamped ceiling, so clamping must be excluded")
check(abs(RM.loaded_mass.to(kilogram).magnitude - 368.0) < 1e-9, "Running-machine loaded mass is 368 kg")
check(AISLE.v_takeover_in_loop < AISLE.v_aisle, "Slow-down before an in-loop takeover")
check(AISLE.mu_oil_film < AISLE.mu_inspected_floor < mu_min < AISLE.mu_dry, "Friction bands are ordered")
check(abs(AISLE.v_aisle.to(meter / second).magnitude - 1.3) < 1e-9, "Signed aisle speed 1.3 m/s")
check(abs(AISLE.d_clear.to(meter).magnitude - 1.10) < 1e-9, "Clear distance 1.10 m")
check(
    abs(AISLE.v_takeover_in_loop.to(meter / second).magnitude - 0.75) < 1e-9,
    "In-loop takeover slow-down 0.75 m/s (Delta_da-charged ceiling, rounded down)",
)
check(abs(AISLE.v_takeover_out_of_loop.to(meter / second).magnitude - 0.15) < 1e-9, "Out-of-loop takeover slow-down 0.15 m/s")
check(abs(AISLE.t_tick.to(millisecond).magnitude - 1.0) < 1e-9, "Permission tick 1 ms")
check(AISLE.t_tick < AISLE.t_lease, "Servo tick sits inside the chunk lease")
check(abs(RM.onboard_payload_capacity.to(kilogram).magnitude - 50.0) < 1e-9, "Tote-rack capacity is 50 kg")
check(
    abs(AISLE.mu_dry - 0.60) < 1e-9 and abs(AISLE.mu_inspected_floor - 0.12) < 1e-9 and abs(AISLE.mu_oil_film - 0.05) < 1e-9,
    "Friction bands 0.60, 0.12, 0.05",
)
check(abs(AISLE.v_latch_approach.to(meter / second).magnitude - 0.03) < 1e-9, "Guarded latch approach 0.03 m/s")
check(abs(AISLE.v_latch_high.to(meter / second).magnitude - 0.10) < 1e-9, "Unsupported latch approach 0.10 m/s")
check(abs(AISLE.f_latch_tripwire.to(newton).magnitude - 15.0) < 1e-9, "Latch tripwire 15 N")
check(abs(AISLE.t_contact_response.to(millisecond).magnitude - 2.0) < 1e-9, "Contact-loop response 2 ms")
check(abs(AISLE.f_latch_limit.to(newton).magnitude - 100.0) < 1e-9, "Latch limit 100 N")
check(abs(AISLE.v_handover.to(meter / second).magnitude - 0.10) < 1e-9, "Handover speed 0.10 m/s")
check(abs(AISLE.f_contact_criterion.to(newton).magnitude - 50.0) < 1e-9, "Handover criterion 50 N")

# ┌── 4. OUTPUT: rendered values ────────────────────────────────────────────────
class ReleaseEnvelope:
    v_restricted = v_restricted  # chosen; read by calc-release-worked-verdict
    v_aisle_str = fmt_velocity(AISLE.v_aisle, unit=meter / second, precision=1)
    v_ceiling_str = fmt_velocity(round(v_ceiling.magnitude, 2) * meter / second, unit=meter / second, precision=2)
    v_takeover_in_str = fmt_velocity(AISLE.v_takeover_in_loop, unit=meter / second, precision=2)
    v_takeover_out_str = fmt_velocity(AISLE.v_takeover_out_of_loop, unit=meter / second, precision=2)
    t_tick_str = fmt_latency(AISLE.t_tick, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    payload_str = fmt_mass(RM.onboard_payload_capacity, unit=kilogram, precision=0)
    m1_str = fmt_mass(RM.loaded_mass, unit=kilogram, precision=0)
    mu_min_str = fmt(round(mu_min, 3), precision=3)
    mu_dry_str = fmt(AISLE.mu_dry, precision=2)
    mu_inspected_str = fmt(AISLE.mu_inspected_floor, precision=2)
    mu_oil_str = fmt(AISLE.mu_oil_film, precision=2)
    v_inspected_ceiling_str = fmt_velocity(round(v_inspected_ceiling.magnitude, 2) * meter / second, unit=meter / second, precision=2)
    v_restricted_str = fmt_velocity(v_restricted, unit=meter / second, precision=0)
    d_clear_str = fmt_length(AISLE.d_clear, unit=meter, precision=2)
    v_latch_str = fmt_velocity(AISLE.v_latch_approach, unit=meter / second, precision=2)
    v_latch_high_str = fmt_velocity(AISLE.v_latch_high, unit=meter / second, precision=2)
    f_trip_str = fmt_force(AISLE.f_latch_tripwire, precision=0)
    t_contact_str = fmt_latency(AISLE.t_contact_response, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    f_latch_limit_str = fmt_force(AISLE.f_latch_limit, precision=0)
    v_handover_str = fmt_velocity(AISLE.v_handover, unit=meter / second, precision=2)
    v_handover_ceiling_str = fmt_velocity(round(v_handover_ceiling.magnitude, 2) * meter / second, unit=meter / second, precision=2)
    v_handover_ceiling_clamped_str = fmt_velocity(round(v_handover_ceiling_clamped.magnitude, 3) * meter / second, unit=meter / second, precision=3)
    f_contact_str = fmt_force(AISLE.f_contact_criterion, precision=0)
```

A release case is scoped by the operating envelope, the target operational design domain (ODD)\index{Operational design domain!release envelope} paired with the machine's own internal hardware, thermal, and timing invariants. A release authorizes a configuration under standing conditions; it does not replace the short execution leases that bound individual action chunks. Site inspections, calibration checks, and per-tick permission checks each run at the cadence required by their own failure mechanism. An unconditional (`UNCOND`) verdict authorizes tracking proposals across the full verified operating envelope (@sec-verification-operating-envelope), a conditional (`COND`) verdict a named subset with restricted kinematics or environmental fences, and a refusal (`REFUSE`) none.\index{Operational design domain!release verdicts} For the mobile manipulator, the operating envelope admits aisle travel at up to `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.v_aisle_str` (chosen; see the Reader Guide) with the tote rack loaded to at most `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.payload_str`, on floors surveyed to a friction coefficient of at least `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.mu_min_str`, past rack ends with at least `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.d_clear_str` of clear distance. It admits door approaches at `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.v_latch_str` and item handovers to the coworker at `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.v_handover_str`.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The operational design domain and its known absences are defined in @sec-data-policy-coverage.
:::

Inside these boundaries the learned neural policy may propose actions across the nominal task envelope, but each action still requires independent, per-tick permission from an isolated safety enforcer. Mode-specific conditions (@tbl-16-odd-invariants) narrow that envelope. The takeover analysis screens an in-loop request at `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.v_takeover_in_str` and an out-of-loop crawl at `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.v_takeover_out_str`; neither is a qualified release limit. The moving in-loop braking blend fails its clearance check, so the base uses its resident stop before transfer (@sec-intervention-authority-transitions). The restricted mode of a `COND` verdict narrows it further: on a floor known only through the site's inspection regime, the machine runs at `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.v_restricted_str`, below the `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.v_inspected_ceiling_str` partial inspected-floor ceiling; admission delay and a positive remaining reserve must still be charged.

The rules in @tbl-16-odd-invariants have priority: refusal conditions override mode-specific restrictions, which override nominal limits. The speed ranges overlap, so these are operating modes rather than disjoint numerical intervals. A stale payload estimate can permit separately supported stationary arm work; an invalid estimate or overload invokes the refusal rule. A conditional state restricts admitted proposals via enforcer clamping. A refusal state revokes the capability token, withdraws motor tracking permission, and commands a validated fallback (@sec-enforcement-fallback-ladder). On-board wheel slip estimation cannot provide prospective clearance guarantees: it detects low friction only *after* wheel slip has begun and traction is lost. A clear oil film ($\mu \approx$ `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.mu_oil_str`) can be visually indistinguishable from dry concrete to the installed cameras. By the time a high-speed vehicle initiates braking on an oil patch and measures slip, it is already kinetically committed to an extended skid. Hence, floor friction must be enforced through site surveys and custodial spill regimes.

Sensor mounting drift can invalidate the localization allowance even when software remains unchanged (@sec-release-calibration-drift). An update that overwrites the measured sensor transforms and joint offsets\index{Over-the-air update!calibration retention} invalidates it just as surely, so the update process must retain and verify those records before restoring tracking authority (@sec-release-modular-safety-cases).

The evidence must also record what happens when operation reaches a boundary. Event-triggered telemetry\index{Edge telemetry!event-triggered buffer}\index{Black-box recorder!pre- and post-trigger capture} retains local traces for later review (@sec-release-data-curation-flywheel), while the permission path enforces the live limits. The table lists the dimensions kept within bounds by runtime monitors or site procedures. Internal conditions from @sec-verification-operating-envelope, such as ambient temperature, rail voltage, and compute load, enter through the fault records trialed at them.

\Needspace{28\baselineskip}

| Envelope Dimension / Invariant | Nominal Envelope ($\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{nom}}$)                                                                           | Conditional Boundary ($\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{cond}}$)                                                                                                                                                                                 | Hard Refusal ($\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{refuse}}$)                                                                                                                                                         | Runtime Monitor & Rate                                                                 | Enforcer Action & Latency                                                      |
|:-------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Aisle Speed**                | $v\le$ `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.v_aisle_str`                                                                             | Preliminary takeover screens: `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.v_takeover_in_str` in-loop and `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.v_takeover_out_str` out-of-loop; rejected in-loop blend requires stop first                                         | Measured speed above the signed `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.v_aisle_str` (ceiling `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.v_ceiling_str`), or invalid speed estimate                                                   | Encoders and IMU, every `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.t_tick_str` permission tick          | Clamp admitted speed; refuse above the signed speed                            |
| **Floor Friction**             | Surveyed $\mu\ge$ `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.mu_min_str` (dry concrete near `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.mu_dry_str`)         | Qualified assessment and maintained site regime ($\mu\ge$ `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.mu_inspected_str`): restricted `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.v_restricted_str`, below the `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.v_inspected_ceiling_str` ceiling | Unsurveyed floor or reported film; a clear oil film ($\mu\approx$ `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.mu_oil_str`) can evade the installed cameras                                                               | Floor survey and site spill procedure; no on-board measurement                         | Restrict speed by floor zone; refuse the aisle                                 |
| **Tote-Rack Payload**          | $0\le m\le$ `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.payload_str`, valid load estimate (total at most `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.m1_str`) | Estimate stale since the last pick: stationary arm tasks only                                                                                                                                                                        | Load above capacity or invalid estimate                                                                                                                                                                | Rack load cells, at each pick                                                          | Refuse aisle transit until re-weighed                                          |
| **Rack-End Clearance**         | Surveyed $D_{\text{clear}}\ge$ `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.d_clear_str` at every rack end                                   | Shorter surveyed clearance: lower signed speed from the same budget                                                                                                                                                                  | Unsurveyed rack end, or obstacle inside the clear distance                                                                                                                                             | Site survey; lidar and navigation camera at frame rate                                 | Speed limit per rack end; stop for a detected obstacle                         |
| **Door Latch Approach**        | $v\le$ `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.v_latch_str`, strike plate at its nominal position                                       | Original policy: nominal plate only; changed recovery candidate needs its own evaluation and release case                                                                                                                            | `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.v_latch_high_str` approach or plate condition outside the selected policy case                                                                                               | Arm contact-force sensing in the `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.t_contact_str` contact loop | Trip at `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.f_trip_str`; refuse the unsupported approach |
| **Coworker Handover**          | TCP speed $\le$ `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.v_handover_str` under `accept_item`                                             | Coworker present without `accept_item`: hold short of the handover point                                                                                                                                                             | TCP speed above the signed `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.v_handover_str` (transient ceiling `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.v_handover_ceiling_str`), or a clamping geometry outside the assessed transient case | Joint encoders every permission tick; arm contact-force sensing                        | Clamp TCP speed; refuse above the signed speed                                 |

: **Operating envelope of the warehouse mobile manipulator**: Refusal rules take priority over restricted-mode rules and nominal limits. Conditional operation requires every relied-on premise to remain supported; stale payload evidence permits only separately supported stationary work, while an invalid estimate or overload refuses. The takeover speeds are preliminary screens, not qualified motion limits. The displayed speed ceilings are partial calculations before dispatch-to-admission delay; signed limits require that delay and a positive reserve. Sensor rates and stopping response are plant validation obligations. {#tbl-16-odd-invariants tbl-colwidths="[16,16,18,18,16,16]"}

The nominal latch row scopes the original policy case. The separately stipulated recovery campaign in @sec-evaluation evaluates a changed candidate on nominal and displaced-plate conditions. That new provenance can support expanded capability, but it does not silently extend this release's contact or timing evidence.

A defensible release claim states its plant, contact geometry, and fault set. The machine's case uses three criteria. The base stops inside the `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.d_clear_str` clear distance before it reaches a person who has stepped out at a rack end, the arm opens the door without exceeding the `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.f_latch_limit_str` latch limit, and a handover never presses on the coworker with more than a chosen `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.f_contact_str` peak force for an assessed contact case. The base's claim protects a stationary person; a person still walking toward the machine is a separate premise, carried by a site crossing rule (@sec-memory-belief-through-occlusion). The release argument must demonstrate which human contacts are excluded before impact, which detected contacts the model covers, and which single faults the independent fallback handles. A stop after contact does not by itself cap the first force peak.

```{python}
#| label: calc-release-biomechanical-impact-envelope
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ HANDOVER CONTACT FORCE AND THE BASE'S STOPPING SPARE
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-release-question (the handover-premise paragraph and the
# │          spare-spent-as-delay paragraph), and the refusal paragraph of
# │          @sec-release-three-verdicts (the deceleration the budget assumes).
# │          The contact-force derivation itself lives in
# │          calc-enforcement-contact-force (@sec-enforcement-intentional-contact);
# │          this cell reads it through calc-release-contact-premises.
# │ Goal: Restate the handover premises release inherits, and show how little
# │       input error the base's finished budget can absorb at aisle speed.
# │ Show: unbraked force at the free-space TCP limit and at the handover speed;
# │       budget and spare at 1.3 m/s; the delay and the deceleration shortfall
# │       that each consume the spare.
# │ How: contact forces read from EnforcementContactForce (free hand: reduced
# │      mass of hand and arm; clamped: the arm's effective mass alone); the
# │      jerk-limited S-curve stop
# │      (calc_scurve_stop_distance; jerk bound = the reference C2 polynomial's
# │      peak jerk at the drive limit) and the three overheads; the break-even
# │      deceleration solves v^2/(2a) + v a/(2j) = braking room with j fixed.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import (
    fmt_mass,
    fmt_stiffness,
    fmt_force,
    fmt_multiple,
    fmt_latency,
    fmt_acceleration,
    fmt_length,
    fmt_velocity,
    fmt_percent,
    fmt_sci_qty,
    check,
)
from mlsysim.physics.robotics import (
    calc_c2_stop_suffix,
    calc_scurve_stop_distance,
)

# ┌── 1. LOAD: the running machine and its site ─────────────────────────────────
RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator  # category: illustrative (running machine)
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle  # category: illustrative (aisle scene; speeds, lease, and tick chosen)

# ┌── 2. EXECUTE: contact forces, then the budget at aisle speed ────────────────
# Contact premises from the enforcement record (calc-release-contact-premises).
m_eff = EnforcementContactForce.m_eff
f_at_tcp_limit = EnforcementContactForce.f_at_tcp_limit
f_ratio = EnforcementContactForce.f_ratio
f_at_handover = EnforcementContactForce.f_handover
f_at_handover_clamped = EnforcementContactForce.f_handover_clamped
v_handover_ceiling = EnforcementContactForce.v_ceiling
v_handover_ceiling_clamped = EnforcementContactForce.v_ceiling_clamped

# Jerk bound: the reference C2 polynomial's peak jerk at the drive limit (@sec-planning-c2-stopping-suffix)
j_brake = calc_c2_stop_suffix(RM.base.max_velocity, AISLE.a_brake)["peak_jerk"].to(meter / second**3)
c2_braking = calc_scurve_stop_distance(AISLE.v_aisle, AISLE.a_brake, j_brake).to(meter)
overhead_loc = AISLE.delta_loc + AISLE.eps_track
d_reaction = (AISLE.v_aisle * AISLE.tau_delay).to(millimeter)
budget_aisle = (d_reaction + c2_braking + overhead_loc + AISLE.delta_margin).to(millimeter)
spare_aisle = (AISLE.d_clear - budget_aisle).to(millimeter)
t_spare = (spare_aisle / AISLE.v_aisle).to(millisecond)
spare_share = (spare_aisle / AISLE.d_clear).to("dimensionless").magnitude
# Deceleration at which the budget exactly fills the clear distance, jerk bound
# fixed. Above a^2/j the S-curve distance is v^2/(2a) + v a/(2j), so setting it
# equal to the braking room gives (v/(2j)) a^2 - room a + v^2/2 = 0; the smaller
# root is the one on the branch where distance falls as a rises (a < sqrt(v j)).
braking_room = (AISLE.d_clear - AISLE.v_aisle * AISLE.tau_delay - overhead_loc - AISLE.delta_margin).to(meter)
_qa = (AISLE.v_aisle / (2 * j_brake)).to(second**2)
_qc = (AISLE.v_aisle**2 / 2).to(meter**2 / second**2)
a_break_even = ((braking_room - (braking_room**2 - 4 * _qa * _qc) ** 0.5) / (2 * _qa)).to(meter / second**2)
a_shortfall = ((AISLE.a_brake - a_break_even) / AISLE.a_brake).to("dimensionless").magnitude

# ┌── 3. GUARD: canon values quoted in the prose ────────────────────────────────
check(abs(m_eff.to(kilogram).magnitude - 12.0) < 1e-9, "Effective contact mass is 12.0 kg")
check(abs(f_at_tcp_limit.magnitude - 207.02) < 0.01, "Transient force at the TCP limit")
check(abs(f_ratio - 4.14) < 0.01, "About 4.1x the 50 N criterion")
check(abs(f_at_handover.magnitude - 20.70) < 0.01, "Transient handover force is 20.7 N")
check(abs(f_at_handover_clamped.magnitude - 94.87) < 0.01, "Clamped handover force is 94.9 N")
check(f_at_handover < AISLE.f_contact_criterion < f_at_handover_clamped, "Transient passes, clamped fails the criterion")
check(abs(v_handover_ceiling.magnitude - 0.2415) < 5e-5, "Transient handover ceiling is 0.24 m/s")
check(abs(v_handover_ceiling_clamped.magnitude - 0.0527) < 5e-5, "Clamped handover ceiling is 0.053 m/s")
check(abs(j_brake.magnitude - 64.0 / 9.0) < 1e-9, "Jerk bound is the reference polynomial's 7.11 m/s^3 peak")
check(abs(budget_aisle.magnitude - 968.9925) < 5e-3, "Finished budget at 1.3 m/s")
check(abs(spare_aisle.magnitude - 131.0075) < 5e-3, "Spare at 1.3 m/s")
check(abs(t_spare.magnitude - 100.775) < 5e-3, "Spare spent as delay is 100.8 ms")
# margin_aisle_budget_spare_envelope.svg fig-alt hand-types the five terms and the spare
check(abs(d_reaction.magnitude - 173.68) < 5e-3, "Reaction travel 173.7 mm at 1.3 m/s")
check(abs(c2_braking.to(millimeter).magnitude - 605.3125) < 5e-3, "S-curve braking 605.3 mm")
check(abs(AISLE.delta_loc.to(millimeter).magnitude - 50.0) < 1e-9, "Localization allowance 50 mm")
check(abs(AISLE.eps_track.to(millimeter).magnitude - 40.0) < 1e-9, "Tracking allowance 40 mm")
check(abs(AISLE.delta_margin.to(millimeter).magnitude - 100.0) < 1e-9, "Physical margin 100 mm")
check(0.11 < spare_share < 0.125, "The spare is about an eighth of the clear distance")
check(AISLE.v_aisle >= a_break_even**2 / j_brake, "Break-even stop stays in the trapezoidal regime")
check(
    abs((calc_scurve_stop_distance(AISLE.v_aisle, a_break_even, j_brake) - braking_room).to(millimeter).magnitude) < 1e-6,
    "At the break-even deceleration the S-curve stop fills the braking room exactly",
)
check(abs(a_break_even.magnitude - 1.386) < 5e-4, "Break-even deceleration is 1.386 m/s^2")
check(abs(a_shortfall - 0.307) < 5e-4, "A 31 percent deceleration shortfall fills the spare")

# ┌── 4. OUTPUT: rendered values ────────────────────────────────────────────────
class BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope:
    v_tcp_str = fmt_velocity(RM.tcp_speed_limit, unit=meter / second, precision=0)
    f_tcp_str = fmt_force(round(f_at_tcp_limit.magnitude) * newton, precision=0)
    f_ratio_mult_str = fmt_multiple(f_ratio, precision=1)
    f_limit_str = fmt_force(AISLE.f_contact_criterion, precision=0)
    v_handover_str = fmt_velocity(AISLE.v_handover, unit=meter / second, precision=2)
    f_handover_str = fmt_force(f_at_handover, precision=1)
    f_handover_clamped_str = fmt_force(f_at_handover_clamped, precision=1)
    v_handover_ceiling_str = fmt_velocity(round(v_handover_ceiling.magnitude, 2) * meter / second, unit=meter / second, precision=2)
    v_handover_ceiling_clamped_str = fmt_velocity(round(v_handover_ceiling_clamped.magnitude, 3) * meter / second, unit=meter / second, precision=3)
    v_aisle_str = fmt_velocity(AISLE.v_aisle, unit=meter / second, precision=1)
    d_clear_str = fmt_length(AISLE.d_clear, unit=meter, precision=2)
    budget_str = fmt_length(budget_aisle, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    spare_str = fmt_length(spare_aisle, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    t_spare_str = fmt_latency(round(t_spare.magnitude, 1) * millisecond, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    a_brake_str = fmt_acceleration(AISLE.a_brake, unit=meter / second**2, precision=0)
    a_break_even_str = fmt_acceleration(a_break_even, unit=meter / second**2, precision=2)
    a_shortfall_pct_str = fmt_percent(round(a_shortfall, 2), precision=0, style="prose")
    # Budget terms for the margin envelope (generator reads the quantities)
    d_reaction = d_reaction
    d_braking = c2_braking.to(millimeter)
    d_loc = AISLE.delta_loc.to(millimeter)
    d_track = AISLE.eps_track.to(millimeter)
    d_margin = AISLE.delta_margin.to(millimeter)
    d_clear = AISLE.d_clear.to(millimeter)
    budget = budget_aisle
    spare = spare_aisle
```

The contact criteria arrive as premises from the enforcement record rather than as calculations release performs. @Sec-enforcement-intentional-contact derives the peak force of an unbraked elastic contact with the coworker's hand (@eq-release-unbraked-force) from the ISO/TS 15066 hand body model[^fn-std-isots15066-biomech] and the arm's effective mass, and the release case takes its results as stated. At the arm's `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.v_tcp_str` free-space limit even the transient model predicts `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.f_tcp_str`, or `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.f_ratio_mult_str` the `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.f_limit_str` criterion, so no unseparated contact is admissible at that speed without a stronger, measured protection argument. For a free hand, which recoils, the criterion admits approach speeds up to `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.v_handover_ceiling_str`, and the chosen `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.v_handover_str` produces `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.f_handover_str`. For a hand clamped against a rack upright or the arm, it admits only `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.v_handover_ceiling_clamped_str`, and the same approach delivers `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.f_handover_clamped_str`, which fails. The handover claim is therefore a transient-contact claim, and release inherits two premises with it: that the body model and effective mass describe this contact, and that the handover geometry excludes clamping. Neither is established by the force calculation; both are premises the release case must evidence.

[^fn-std-isots15066-biomech]: **ISO/TS 15066 Values as Case Criteria**\index{ISO/TS 15066!case criterion}: The document supplies a body model and body-region force and pressure data for transient and quasi-static contact [@isots15066], and its requirements for collaborative applications now sit in ISO 10218-2:2025 [@iso10218part2]. The `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.f_limit_str` handover criterion is none of those tabulated values and is not an injury boundary. The site assessment chooses it for one body region, contact type, and geometry, so a change to any of the three reopens the claim instead of inheriting its margin.

The base's claim is a budget rather than a single force, and the delay components this chapter must evidence are the lease path and the observation age that its claims name. At the `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.v_aisle_str` aisle speed, the partial budget before dispatch-to-admission delay (@tbl-enforcement-stopping-budget) is `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.budget_str` against the `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.d_clear_str` clear distance, leaving a critical spare of only `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.spare_str`. That spare must first pay for dispatch-to-admission work, which the illustrative calculation has not yet charged. Remaining reserve must cover the other required uncertainties; it is not all available as extra waiting time. An unbudgeted pipeline delay of `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.t_spare_str` spends that partial spare entirely; this is not an additional full handover allowance once admission work and required reserve are charged (@sec-intervention-authority-transitions). The same partial spare is exhausted if loaded braking reaches only `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.a_break_even_str` under the same jerk bound, a deceleration shortfall of `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.a_shortfall_pct_str` below the `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.a_brake_str` the budget assumes. A stopping claim whose inputs are unmeasured cannot demonstrate that its spare survives these real-world compounding errors.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/margin_aisle_budget_spare_envelope.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="One horizontal stacked bar in millimeters: reaction travel of 173.7 millimeters, braking of 605.3 millimeters, then allowances of 50 for localization, 40 for tracking, and 100 millimeters of physical margin, followed by a dashed box for the 131.0 millimeters spare that ends at a red line marking the 1.10 meters clear distance."}

*The partial budget leaves only `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.spare_str` of the `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.d_clear_str` clear distance spare.*
:::

The release question for the mobile manipulator has become three bounded criteria: the base stops inside the clear distance, the arm opens the door under the latch limit, and an item handover stays under the contact criterion. Each calculation inherits premises about deceleration, latency, and contact stiffness that need physical evidence and can lapse in service. A safety case exposes those dependencies so a reviewer can decide which operating claims they support.

## Safety Cases and Claims {#sec-release-safety-cases-claims}

A photograph of a clear aisle cannot establish that the loaded base stops inside it. That claim depends on clearance, braking capability, and response timing, each supported by evidence gathered under stated conditions. A safety case connects those premises to the claim so the release reviewer can identify what is supported and what remains untested.

### Assurance argument grammar and warrants {#sec-release-assurance-grammar}

A safety case is reviewable only if its structure is written down in a form another engineer can check link by link. Two notations are in common use, and they describe the same structure. The **claim-argument-evidence (CAE)**\index{Claim-argument-evidence!notation} framework separates three things: the *claim*, an assertion about the machine that is either true or false; the *argument*, the reasoning that connects the claim to what was measured; and the *evidence*, the retained measurements themselves [@bishop1998methodology; @bloomfield2014building]. **Goal Structuring Notation (GSN)**\index{Goal Structuring Notation!elements} draws the same structure as a graph, in which goals (claims) decompose through strategies (arguments) into solutions (evidence items), and context and assumption nodes state the conditions under which each link holds [@kelly1998arguing; @kelly2004goal]. The fault records of @sec-verification-contract-matrix enter the graph as solutions, each under the claim its header names. Release uses the notation to decide, so the safety case of \ref{dfn-release-goal-structured-safety-case}\index{Claim-argument-evidence safety case!argument structure} now carries a verdict. Its structure descends from Stephen Toulmin's analysis of arguments[^fn-toulmin-argument-anatomy] [@toulmin1958uses], and ANSI/UL 4600 requires a goal-based safety case of this kind for autonomous products [@ul4600; @koopman2023ul4600]. Published industrial cases exist; Waymo's, for its driverless ride-hailing service, argues the absence of unreasonable risk from layered, dynamic, and credible perspectives on safety, and it argues separately that its acceptance criteria are sufficient and that their evaluation is credible [@favaro2023building]. Its top-level claim $C_0$ names a testable physical property, such as keeping the base's stopping distance within surveyed clearance ($d_{\text{stop}} \le D_{\text{clear}}$) or limiting contact force ($F_{\text{contact}} \le F_{\text{limit}}$). Supporting claims identify the conditions needed for that result, and evidence records support those claims. Representing these links as a directed acyclic graph (DAG) makes their dependencies explicit: the reviewer can follow a claim toward its supporting observations without circular reasoning. The graph also records the operating assumptions under which each link holds.

[^fn-toulmin-argument-anatomy]: **Toulmin's Argument Anatomy**\index{Toulmin, Stephen!argument model}: *The Uses of Argument* splits practical reasoning into claim, data, warrant, backing, qualifier, and rebuttal. Safety cases kept that anatomy. Evidence plays the data, stated confidence plays the qualifier, and the rebuttal becomes the defeater that adversarial review hunts for (@sec-release-adversarial-review).

The structural integrity of this engineering assertion DAG hinges on strictly distinguishing evidence from demonstration. A **demonstration**\index{Demonstration!vs. evidence} is a record of successful task execution over an uncharacterized test distribution, such as a long run of clean door openings with the strike plate always at its nominal position or a thousand collision-free warehouse aisle transits. It measures mean performance but bounds neither the tail nor the failure modes outside the sampled trajectory. In contrast, evidence is a falsifiable, calibrated artifact with quantified uncertainty bounds, such as an execution-time distribution captured on a logic analyzer together with the separate analysis supporting a worst-case execution time (WCET) bound, loaded vehicle stopping trials across degraded friction regimes, or a hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) fault-injection trace that drives the machine to the physical boundary of its envelope. Evidence requirements follow the claim: nominal trials can support performance in their sampled conditions, and calibration records can support the measured sensor geometry. Neither must stress every physical boundary to be useful. A worst-response or envelope-boundary claim needs the additional coverage, uncertainty analysis, and warrant that establish that stronger result.

Connecting evidence to a claim requires a **warrant**\index{Warrant!inferential rule}, the inferential rule stating why the empirical data support the assertion. For a learned neural policy, the warrant is inductive, reasoning from failure-free test episodes to future operational reliability. However, the exposure wall of @sec-evaluation-trial-limits demonstrates why inductive warrants cannot carry a catastrophic hazard claim alone: under the Poisson zero-event rule ($T \ge 3.0/\lambda$), demonstrating an ultra-reliable failure rate ($10^{-9}$ per operating hour) would require billions of operating hours without a single incident [@butler1993infeasibility; @kalra2016driving]. Which rate is acceptable in the first place is a separate judgment that no quantity of trials makes for itself [@koopman2022how]. The safety case must therefore incorporate deterministic architectural warrants, grounding the top-level claim in an independent permission path (@sec-enforcement) that enforces Control Barrier Functions (CBFs) to clamp actuator commands and command an assessed safe stop whenever a learned proposal approaches the boundary of the viable set $\mathcal{C}_{\text{viable}}$. That architectural warrant narrows the claim rather than escaping the exposure wall, since the permission path protects only against the specific hazards it monitors and can arrest within physical stopping limits (@sec-frontier-method-limits). The learned proposer still needs its own argument for the service it delivers. ISO/PAS 8800:2024 extends road-vehicle safety practice to AI components, covering the AI safety lifecycle, the data an AI element is trained and tested on, and the assurance argument for that element [@iso8800]. Outside road vehicles, the Assurance of Machine Learning in Autonomous Systems (AMLAS) guidance supplies safety-case patterns and a process for building that argument while the component is developed [@hawkins2021amlas]. In this book's architecture the permission path carries the hazard argument for the monitored hazards, with its formal protective claim resting on the rated watchdog, the certified drive functions, and the safety scanner (@sec-release-standards-map), so the proposer's argument bears mainly on capability and on the hazards the permission path does not monitor.

### Contextual assumptions and the weakest link {#sec-release-contextual-assumptions}

A stopping trial conducted in a well-lit aisle also depends on the sensing conditions there. Moving the same machine into a dim aisle can change observation age even when its brakes perform exactly as before. The argument must name such contextual assumptions so a valid measurement is not applied outside the conditions that give it meaning.

```{python}
#| label: calc-release-low-light-age
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ AN UNSTATED LIGHTING ASSUMPTION IN THE STOPPING BUDGET
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-release-safety-cases-claims (contextual-assumptions paragraph).
# │ Goal: Show how a lighting change the budget never named ages the navigation
# │       camera's image, and what it would cost the aisle budget's spare
# │       if the age check did not refuse the frames.
# │ Show: nominal and low-light exposure, the added observation age, the added
# │       travel at aisle speed, and its share of the spare.
# │ How: perception age is timed from mid-exposure (AISLE.perception_age), so a
# │      longer exposure adds half its increase; spare from the jerk-limited
# │      S-curve stop (calc_scurve_stop_distance; jerk bound = the reference C2
# │      polynomial's peak jerk at the drive limit) and the three overheads.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_latency, fmt_length, fmt_velocity, fmt_percent, check
from mlsysim.physics.robotics import calc_c2_stop_suffix, calc_scurve_stop_distance

# ┌── 1. LOAD: the running machine, plus one chapter-local input ────────────────
RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator  # category: illustrative (running machine)
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle  # category: illustrative (aisle scene; speeds, lease, and tick chosen)
low_light_exposure_factor = 2.0  # category: illustrative (scenario assumption: a dim aisle doubles the exposure)

# ┌── 2. EXECUTE ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
t_exp_nominal = RM.nav_camera.exposure_time.to(millisecond)
t_exp_low = (low_light_exposure_factor * t_exp_nominal).to(millisecond)
dt_age = ((t_exp_low - t_exp_nominal) / 2).to(millisecond)  # mid-exposure timestamp
d_added = (AISLE.v_aisle * dt_age).to(millimeter)
# Jerk bound: the reference C2 polynomial's peak jerk at the drive limit (@sec-planning-c2-stopping-suffix)
j_brake = calc_c2_stop_suffix(RM.base.max_velocity, AISLE.a_brake)["peak_jerk"].to(meter / second**3)
budget = (
    AISLE.v_aisle * AISLE.tau_delay
    + calc_scurve_stop_distance(AISLE.v_aisle, AISLE.a_brake, j_brake)
    + AISLE.delta_loc
    + AISLE.eps_track
    + AISLE.delta_margin
).to(millimeter)
spare = (AISLE.d_clear - budget).to(millimeter)
share_of_spare = (d_added / spare).to("dimensionless").magnitude

# ┌── 3. GUARD ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
check(abs(t_exp_nominal.magnitude - 16.0) < 1e-9, "Navigation-camera exposure 16 ms")
check(abs(dt_age.magnitude - 8.0) < 1e-9, "Low light adds 8 ms of observation age")
check(abs(d_added.magnitude - 10.4) < 1e-9, "10.4 mm of added travel at 1.3 m/s")
check(abs(spare.magnitude - 131.0075) < 5e-3, "Spare at 1.3 m/s")
check(abs(share_of_spare - 0.079) < 5e-3, "About 8 percent of the spare")

# ┌── 4. OUTPUT ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
class ReleaseLowLight:
    t_exp_nominal_str = fmt_latency(t_exp_nominal, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_exp_low_str = fmt_latency(t_exp_low, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    dt_age_str = fmt_latency(dt_age, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    v_aisle_str = fmt_velocity(AISLE.v_aisle, unit=meter / second, precision=1)
    d_added_str = fmt_length(d_added, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    spare_str = fmt_length(spare, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    share_str = fmt_percent(round(share_of_spare * 100) / 100.0, precision=0, style="prose")
```

When an operating assumption remains unstated, it is guarded only by whatever secondary check happens to sit downstream in the execution pipeline. In the mobile manipulator's stopping budget, the warrant assumes that warehouse aisles maintain sufficient ambient illumination for the navigation camera's nominal exposure. Suppose a dim aisle doubles that exposure from `{python} ReleaseLowLight.t_exp_nominal_str` to `{python} ReleaseLowLight.t_exp_low_str`. Because an image's age is timed from mid-exposure, each observation arrives `{python} ReleaseLowLight.dt_age_str` older than the budget charges, which unchecked would carry the base another `{python} ReleaseLowLight.d_added_str` at the `{python} ReleaseLowLight.v_aisle_str` aisle speed, about `{python} ReleaseLowLight.share_str` of the budget's `{python} ReleaseLowLight.spare_str` spare. The admission age check refuses those frames instead. An active chunk can continue only while its own evidence and lease remain valid; otherwise the base stops in an aisle the case assumed it could run. The team meets its lighting assumption as unexplained lost service, and only a check that the case never tied to lighting kept it from becoming a silent loss of clearance.

An assumption that no runtime check sees has no such backstop. Sensor mounting drift can introduce a spatial offset while every image still passes its age check. The case must name both the localization allowance and the evidence that keeps the physical sensor geometry within it. Treating fresh telemetry as sufficient evidence of correct geometry leaves that warrant unsupported.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ Epistemic assumptions embedded within safety case warrants are critically interrogated in @sec-frontier-epistemic-limits.
:::

```{python}
#| label: calc-release-argument-confidence
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ HOW CONFIDENCE COMBINES IN A SAFETY ARGUMENT
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-release-contextual-assumptions (the conjunctive and
# │          multi-legged argument paragraphs).
# │ Goal: Show that doubt accumulates across required premises, and that two
# │       independent legs can support a claim better than either leg alone.
# │ Show: confidence in a conjunction of n required premises; confidence in a
# │       claim supported by either of two independent legs.
# │ How: independent premises; conjunction = product of confidences
# │      (calc_conjunctive_confidence); two independent legs fail together
# │      with probability (1-p1)(1-p2) (calc_multilegged_confidence).
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim.physics import calc_conjunctive_confidence, calc_multilegged_confidence
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, check

# ┌── 1. LOAD: chapter-local inputs (a teaching illustration, not a machine value)
p_premise = 0.99  # category: illustrative (confidence in each required premise)
n_premises = 10  # category: illustrative (number of required premises)
p_leg = 0.90  # category: illustrative (confidence in each of two independent legs)

# ┌── 2. EXECUTE ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
p_conjunction = calc_conjunctive_confidence([p_premise] * n_premises)
p_two_legs = calc_multilegged_confidence([p_leg, p_leg])

# ┌── 3. GUARD ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
check(abs(p_conjunction - 0.904) < 5e-4, "Ten premises at 0.99 give about 0.90")
check(p_conjunction < p_premise, "The conjunction is weaker than its weakest premise")
check(abs(p_two_legs - 0.99) < 1e-9, "Two independent legs at 0.90 give 0.99")
check(p_two_legs > p_leg, "Independent legs support the claim better than either leg")

# ┌── 4. OUTPUT ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
class ReleaseArgumentConfidence:
    p_premise_str = fmt(p_premise, precision=2)
    n_premises_str = fmt(n_premises, precision=0)
    p_conjunction_str = fmt(round(p_conjunction, 2), precision=2)
    p_leg_str = fmt(p_leg, precision=2)
    p_two_legs_str = fmt(round(p_two_legs, 2), precision=2)
```

A safety case is not an aggregate scorecard in which strength in one branch compensates for a deficit in another. High accuracy on an object recognition benchmark does not offset an uncharacterized latency tail on the CAN-FD bus, nor does extensive policy simulation offset missing brake-wear data. When every child claim is *required*, the argument is conjunctive, and it is no stronger than its weakest required premise. It is usually weaker, because doubt about independent premises accumulates. If each of `{python} ReleaseArgumentConfidence.n_premises_str` required premises holds with confidence `{python} ReleaseArgumentConfidence.p_premise_str`, the conjunction holds with only about `{python} ReleaseArgumentConfidence.p_conjunction_str`, below every one of them. The base's stopping claim is conjunctive in this sense: clear distance, credible deceleration, brake onset, observation age, and the localization and tracking allowances all enter one budget, and a failed warrant in any of them invalidates the root claim however well the others are evidenced. The adjudicator therefore looks not at the volume of supporting artifacts but at the least supported required premise, and at how many premises share the claim.

The rule has one principled exception. An argument can support a claim through two *independent* legs, either of which suffices, so that the claim fails only if both fail [@bloomfield2003multilegged]. If each of two independent legs holds with confidence `{python} ReleaseArgumentConfidence.p_leg_str`, the claim holds with about `{python} ReleaseArgumentConfidence.p_two_legs_str`, above either leg. The book's architecture is built as such an argument for the hazards the enforcer monitors. The policy's evaluation evidence is one leg, and the independent permission path that admits each proposal is the other, so a policy error alone does not violate the stopping or contact invariant. The exception rests entirely on independence.[^fn-diverse-legs-independence] C5 of @tbl-16-cae-scorecard is the claim that the two legs share no processor, memory channel, power rail, or sensor stream whose failure defeats both; if C5 fails, the legs collapse into a single conjunction. The enforcer leg is itself conjunctive in its physical premises, so C1 to C4 must each hold for it to stand. Diverse legs protect a claim against policy error; they never excuse a missing brake or timing premise.

[^fn-diverse-legs-independence]: **Independence of Diverse Legs**\index{Design diversity!common-mode failure}: When independently written versions of one program were run on the same inputs, they failed together far more often than independent failure predicts, and the experiment rejected the independence hypothesis statistically [@knight1986experimental]. Diversity in design does not by itself give independence in failure. C5 must therefore test the shared processor, rail, and sensor paths rather than assume that the two legs fail independently.

### Argument-to-plant alignment and claim adjudication {#sec-release-argument-plant-alignment}

The warehouse machine's stopping calculation already names its brake onset, deceleration, and observation age. The release reviewer must determine which of those inputs has been measured on the proposed configuration. Correct arithmetic on illustrative inputs establishes a conditional result; it cannot establish that the physical machine satisfies the premises.

```{python}
#| label: calc-release-claims
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ THE SIX RELEASE CLAIMS ON THE RUNNING MACHINE
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-release-safety-cases-claims (scorecard lead-in) and
# │          @tbl-16-cae-scorecard.
# │ Goal: Instance claims C1-C6 on the warehouse mobile manipulator.
# │ Show: base budget at aisle speed against the clear distance; latch force at
# │       brake command, remaining compression, and the arm stop it requires;
# │       mug pick and handover speeds with the handover ceiling and force;
# │       renewal-to-onset time; enforcer WCET and deadline; friction needed
# │       for a_brake; observation age; the handover deadline T_latest at the
# │       in-loop takeover slow-down and at aisle speed.
# │ How: RM/AISLE fields; the jerk-limited S-curve stop (calc_scurve_stop_distance;
# │      jerk bound = the reference C2 polynomial's peak jerk at the drive limit);
# │      latch and handover contact premises from EnforcementContactForce
# │      (calc-release-contact-premises).
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, fmt_force, fmt_mass, fmt_latency, fmt_acceleration, fmt_length, fmt_velocity, check
from mlsysim.physics.robotics import (
    calc_c2_stop_suffix,
    calc_scurve_stop_distance,
)

# ┌── 1. LOAD: the running machine and its site ─────────────────────────────────
RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator  # category: illustrative (running machine)
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle  # category: illustrative (aisle scene; speeds, lease, and tick chosen)
g_std = (1 * ureg.standard_gravity).to(meter / second**2)  # category: datasheet (standard gravity, a defined physical constant; Pint)

# ┌── 2. EXECUTE: one warrant quantity per claim ────────────────────────────────
# Jerk bound: the reference C2 polynomial's peak jerk at the drive limit (@sec-planning-c2-stopping-suffix)
j_brake = calc_c2_stop_suffix(RM.base.max_velocity, AISLE.a_brake)["peak_jerk"].to(meter / second**3)
overheads = (AISLE.delta_loc + AISLE.eps_track + AISLE.delta_margin).to(millimeter)
# C1 base: finished budget at aisle speed.
budget_aisle = (AISLE.v_aisle * AISLE.tau_delay + calc_scurve_stop_distance(AISLE.v_aisle, AISLE.a_brake, j_brake) + overheads).to(millimeter)
spare_aisle = (AISLE.d_clear - budget_aisle).to(millimeter)
# C1 door: force at brake command and the arm stop that keeps it under the limit.
f_cmd = EnforcementContactForce.f_cmd
x_remaining = EnforcementContactForce.x_rem
a_arm_needed = EnforcementContactForce.a_arm
# C1 handover: transient (free-hand) force at the handover speed, ISO hand body model.
f_handover = EnforcementContactForce.f_handover
# C2: last valid renewal to brake onset.
t_renewal_to_onset = (AISLE.t_lease + AISLE.t_tick + AISLE.t_bus + AISLE.t_brake_onset).to(millisecond)
# C3: friction the credible deceleration needs.
mu_min = (AISLE.a_brake / g_std).to("dimensionless").magnitude
v_handover_ceiling = EnforcementContactForce.v_ceiling
# C6: an unacknowledged handover falls back by the spare spent as time, at the
# in-loop takeover slow-down (operative) and at aisle speed (a policy request).
t_timeout = (spare_aisle / AISLE.v_aisle).to(millisecond)
budget_takeover = (
    AISLE.v_takeover_in_loop * AISLE.tau_delay + calc_scurve_stop_distance(AISLE.v_takeover_in_loop, AISLE.a_brake, j_brake) + overheads
).to(millimeter)
spare_takeover = (AISLE.d_clear - budget_takeover).to(millimeter)
t_latest_takeover = (spare_takeover / AISLE.v_takeover_in_loop).to(millisecond)

# ┌── 3. GUARD: canon values quoted in the table ────────────────────────────────
check(abs(budget_aisle.magnitude - 968.9925) < 5e-3, "C1 base budget at 1.3 m/s")
check(budget_aisle < AISLE.d_clear, "C1 budget fits inside the clear distance")
check(abs(f_cmd.magnitude - 39.0) < 1e-9, "C1 latch force at brake command")
check(abs(x_remaining.magnitude - 0.1525) < 1e-6, "C1 remaining compression 0.15 mm")
check(abs(a_arm_needed.magnitude - 2.95) < 0.005, "C1 arm stop premise about 3 m/s^2 (computed 2.95)")
check(abs(f_handover.magnitude - 20.70) < 0.01, "C1 transient handover force 20.7 N")
check(f_handover < AISLE.f_contact_criterion, "C1 handover force under the criterion")
check(abs(t_renewal_to_onset.magnitude - 82.0) < 1e-9, "C2 renewal-to-onset 82 ms")
check(AISLE.enforcer_wcet < AISLE.enforcer_deadline < AISLE.t_tick, "C2 WCET < deadline < tick")
check(abs(mu_min - 0.204) < 5e-4, "C3 friction floor 0.204")
check(abs(AISLE.perception_age.to(millisecond).magnitude - 51.6) < 1e-9, "C4 age 51.6 ms")
check(abs(t_timeout.magnitude - 100.775) < 5e-3, "C6 fallback by 100.8 ms at 1.3 m/s")
check(abs(spare_takeover.magnitude - 563.71) < 0.05, "C6 spare 563.7 mm at the 0.75 m/s slow-down")
check(abs(t_latest_takeover.magnitude - 751.6) < 0.05, "C6 fallback by 751.6 ms at 0.75 m/s")
check(abs(RM.tcp_speed_limit.to(meter / second).magnitude - 1.0) < 1e-9, "C1 mug pick under the 1.0 m/s TCP limit")
check(abs(v_handover_ceiling.magnitude - 0.2415) < 5e-5, "C1 transient handover ceiling 0.24 m/s")

# ┌── 4. OUTPUT: rendered values ────────────────────────────────────────────────
class ReleaseClaims:
    budget_str = fmt_length(budget_aisle, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    v_aisle_str = fmt_velocity(AISLE.v_aisle, unit=meter / second, precision=1)
    d_clear_str = fmt_length(AISLE.d_clear, unit=meter, precision=2)
    f_cmd_str = fmt_force(f_cmd, precision=0)
    x_remaining_str = fmt_length(round(x_remaining.magnitude, 2) * millimeter, unit=millimeter, precision=2)
    a_arm_str = fmt_acceleration(round(a_arm_needed.magnitude) * meter / second**2, unit=meter / second**2, precision=0)
    f_latch_limit_str = fmt_force(AISLE.f_latch_limit, precision=0)
    f_handover_str = fmt_force(f_handover, precision=1)
    v_handover_str = fmt_velocity(AISLE.v_handover, unit=meter / second, precision=2)
    f_contact_str = fmt_force(AISLE.f_contact_criterion, precision=0)
    m1_str = fmt_mass(RM.loaded_mass, unit=kilogram, precision=0)
    t_renewal_to_onset_str = fmt_latency(t_renewal_to_onset, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    wcet_str = fmt_latency(AISLE.enforcer_wcet, unit=microsecond, precision=0)
    deadline_str = fmt_latency(AISLE.enforcer_deadline, unit=microsecond, precision=0)
    mu_min_str = fmt(round(mu_min, 3), precision=3)
    t_age_str = fmt_latency(AISLE.perception_age, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    t_timeout_str = fmt_latency(round(t_timeout.magnitude, 1) * millisecond, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    t_latest_takeover_str = fmt_latency(round(t_latest_takeover.magnitude, 1) * millisecond, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    v_takeover_in_str = fmt_velocity(AISLE.v_takeover_in_loop, unit=meter / second, precision=2)
    v_tcp_str = fmt_velocity(RM.tcp_speed_limit, unit=meter / second, precision=0)
    v_handover_ceiling_str = fmt_velocity(round(v_handover_ceiling.magnitude, 2) * meter / second, unit=meter / second, precision=2)
```

For the mobile manipulator's collaborative manipulation tasks, biomechanical limits inform the contact force case once the assertion names the contacted body region, contact type, pressure distribution, impact geometry, and measurement method [@iso10218part2]. The mobile base's claims, which constitute the core of the release argument, are structured directly from its empirical stopping distance budget and site survey records. Two distinctions borrowed from road-vehicle practice organize the fault side of the argument. Functional safety addresses hazards caused by malfunctions, whether from random hardware faults or from systematic faults in design and software [@iso26262]. The safety of the intended functionality (SOTIF) addresses hazards that arise with no fault at all, from insufficiencies of specification or performance, such as a detector that misses a coworker half hidden behind a stretch-wrapped pallet [@iso21448]. Each leaf of the release argument is verified against a test bench before it can gate motor authority. The standards that actually govern this machine are machinery standards, which @sec-release-standards-map maps to the parts of the machine they cover.

The claim-argument-evidence scorecard in @tbl-16-cae-scorecard states six claims and pairs each physical warrant with its adjudication on this book's evidence. Claim C3 shows the decision: an oil film can defeat braking traction, so nominal model accuracy cannot justify an unrestricted verdict. A physically realizable condition that invalidates a warrant in this way is its **defeater**\index{Defeaters!definition} [@goodenough2013eliminative], and @sec-release-adversarial-review turns the search for defeaters into a review method. Claim C6 stands only on the fault records that test the four authority rules @sec-intervention-authority-log hands over (A1–A4).

@Fig-16-argument-graph draws the same six claims as a graph. It splits C1 into its three contact cases, hangs each claim's premises off it as leaves marked by the status of their evidence, and attaches the oil-film defeater to the claim it attacks. No leaf is yet measured on the proposed configuration, which is why every row of the scorecard reads `REFUSE`.

```{python}
#| label: calc-release-argument-graph-guard
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ ARGUMENT GRAPH LABELS (FIGURE GUARD)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @fig-16-argument-graph (fig16_argument_graph.svg)
# │
# │ Goal: Keep the hand-drawn premise leaves in step with calc-release-claims.
# │ Show: 969.0 mm budget, 131.0 mm spare, 39 N latch force, 0.15 mm, 3 m/s^2,
# │       20.7 N handover force, 82 ms renewal-to-onset, 250/400 µs WCET and
# │       deadline, mu 0.204 and 0.60, 51.6 ms age.
# │ How: format the scenario and ReleaseClaims quantities and require each
# │      label string in the SVG.
# │
# │ Imports: (none)
# │ Exports: (none; guard only)
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import os as _os
from mlsysim.fmt import check

_svg_rel = "images/svg/fig16_argument_graph.svg"
_svg_path = next(_p for _p in (_svg_rel, "books/vol4/16_release/" + _svg_rel, "vol4/16_release/" + _svg_rel) if _os.path.exists(_p))
with open(_svg_path) as _f:
    _svg = _f.read()

_labels = [
    f"{budget_aisle.magnitude:.1f} mm of {AISLE.d_clear.to(meter).magnitude:.2f} m clear",
    f"spare {spare_aisle.magnitude:.1f} mm at {AISLE.v_aisle.to(meter / second).magnitude:.1f} m/s",
    f"{AISLE.a_brake.to(meter / second**2).magnitude:.0f} m/s², onset {AISLE.t_brake_onset.to(millisecond).magnitude:.0f} ms",
    f"tracking {AISLE.eps_track.to(millimeter).magnitude:.0f} mm, local. {AISLE.delta_loc.to(millimeter).magnitude:.0f} mm",
```
