```{python}
    f"{f_cmd.to(newton).magnitude:.0f} N at onset ≤ {AISLE.f_latch_limit.to(newton).magnitude:.0f} N",
    f"latch, guarded {AISLE.v_latch_approach.to(meter / second).magnitude:.2f} m/s",
    f"arm stops within {x_remaining.to(millimeter).magnitude:.2f} mm",
    f"needs about {a_arm_needed.to(meter / second**2).magnitude:.0f} m/s²",
    f"{f_handover.magnitude:.1f} N ≤ {AISLE.f_contact_criterion.to(newton).magnitude:.0f} N at {AISLE.v_handover.to(meter / second).magnitude:.2f} m/s",
    f"onset ≤ {t_renewal_to_onset.magnitude:.0f} ms after renewal",
    f"WCET {AISLE.enforcer_wcet.to(microsecond).magnitude:.0f} µs &lt; {AISLE.enforcer_deadline.to(microsecond).magnitude:.0f} µs",
    f"floor μ ≥ {mu_min:.3f}, every aisle",
    f"dry-floor survey value {AISLE.mu_dry:.2f}",
    f"dispatch age {AISLE.perception_age.to(millisecond).magnitude:.1f} ms",
]
for _lab in _labels:
    check(_lab in _svg, f"argument graph label is stale or missing: {_lab}")
```

: **Claim-argument-evidence review for the warehouse mobile manipulator**: Six claims and their adjudication on this book's evidence. Displayed stopping distances and waiting allowances are partial calculations; admission work, physical response, and required reserve must be charged at their own events. A failed or unknown branch cannot be compensated by nominal model accuracy. {#tbl-16-cae-scorecard tbl-colwidths="[14,58,28]"}

::: {#chk-release-claim-argument-evidence-and-inductive-warrants .callout-checkpoint title="Safety case decomposition and warrants"}

Before presenting a safety case for adjudication, test its structure:

- [ ] **Top-level claim falsifiability**: Can you state the top-level claim as a falsifiable physical proposition, such as a stop inside the clear distance, rather than an aspiration?
- [ ] **Warrant validity**: Can you name the warrant connecting each test bench to the claim above it, and the premises under which that warrant holds?
- [ ] **Defeater enumeration**: Can you show where a defeater such as lens fouling or bus arbitration collisions appears in the argument graph?
- [ ] **Evidentiary provenance**: Can you trace every terminal evidence node to a signed test trace and a current calibration?
:::

The scorecard separates a physical requirement from the evidence available to support it. The release verdict must preserve that distinction across the whole case: a supported branch cannot compensate for a missing premise elsewhere.

### The standards map for the running machine {#sec-release-standards-map}

A reviewer who signs the warehouse machine's release must also establish which published requirements govern which part of the machine and which section produced the evidence each one asks for, a question the scorecard does not ask. The machine is an industrial mobile manipulator, not a road vehicle, so its route runs through machinery standards. ISO 12100 sets the frame. A documented risk assessment identifies hazards, estimates their risk, and reduces it first by inherently safe design, then by safeguarding, and last by information for use [@iso12100]. Every other document in @tbl-16-standards-map governs one part of that reduction. The road-vehicle and autonomy documents enter as borrowed method, because they supply vocabulary for learned components and for safety cases that the machinery standards do not yet provide in full.

: **Standards map for the warehouse mobile manipulator (as of 2026)**: Each document, its edition, what it governs, the part of the running machine it covers, and the section that produces the evidence it asks for. Machinery standards form the certification route; the road-vehicle and autonomy documents are borrowed method. Editions and dates change; a later printing should refresh this table. {#tbl-16-standards-map tbl-colwidths="[17,13,28,24,18]"}

Two rows of the map need a sentence each, because the running machine sits at the edge of their scope. ISO 10218-2:2025 covers the arm and its application but excludes the hazards of mobility when a manipulator is integrated with a mobile platform [@iso10218part2], and a manipulator on a mobile platform is exactly what the warehouse machine is. ISO 3691-4 covers the base as a driverless truck. The document that assesses the arm moving on the base as one machine is ANSI/A3 R15.08. A manipulator on the base makes the machine an IMR Type C, and Part 2 sets the requirements for integrating it into a system and an application [@ansi1508part1; @ansi1508part2]. Where R15.08 does not apply, the combined hazards still belong to the machine's own ISO 12100 risk assessment.

The second is which part of the permission path carries a rating. In this book's architecture only a narrow part does. The safety MCU's lease-expiry and heartbeat watchdog, which fires Safe Torque Off or Safe Stop 1 on the drives when renewals stop arriving, is a rated safety function, developed to a performance level under ISO 13849-1 or a safety integrity level under IEC 61508. The admission checks that decide whether a learned proposal is accepted (the barrier projection, the feasibility check, and the freshness logic beyond the watchdog) carry no rating. For the hazards they monitor, the certified drive functions and the safety scanner carry the formal protective claim (@sec-enforcement-certified-functions). The release argument may lean on the admission checks for useful service, but a hazard claim that rests on them alone is a premise, not a certified function.

Law reaches the machine through product-safety regulation rather than through a separate regime for AI. In the European Union, the Machinery Regulation applies from 20 January 2027 [@eu2023machinery]. Two of its provisions bear directly on release. It lists safety components with fully or partially self-evolving behavior that use machine learning to ensure safety functions, and machinery with such embedded systems, among the products whose conformity assessment[^fn-conformity-assessment-route] requires a third party. It also defines a *substantial modification*\index{Substantial modification!Machinery Regulation} as a change made after the machine is placed on the market, by physical or digital means, that the manufacturer did not foresee and that creates a new hazard or increases an existing risk enough to require new protective measures; whoever makes such a change takes on the manufacturer's obligations. An over-the-air update is a digital means, which is how @sec-release-modular-safety-cases enters the law. The AI Act, Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 [@eu2024aiact], was amended in July 2026 by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 [@eu2026omnibus]. The amendment moved the Machinery Regulation from Section A to Section B of the AI Act's Annex I, so AI embedded in machinery is regulated mainly through the Machinery Regulation, and it requires the Commission to add health and safety requirements for such AI systems to that regulation by delegated acts that apply by 2 August 2028. Because the machine takes its updates over a network, it is also a product with digital elements under the Cyber Resilience Act, Regulation (EU) 2024/2847, which applies from 11 December 2027, with its duty to report actively exploited vulnerabilities applying from 11 September 2026 [@eu2024cra]. It requires that vulnerabilities can be fixed through security updates over a declared support period, normally at least five years, and machinery that contains such digital elements must meet both it and the Machinery Regulation. None of these dates changes the engineering argument. They set when a regulator will ask to see it.

[^fn-conformity-assessment-route]: **Conformity Assessment**\index{Conformity assessment!Machinery Regulation}: This is the procedure by which a manufacturer demonstrates that a product meets the regulation's essential health and safety requirements before affixing the CE marking [@eu2023machinery]. For most machinery the manufacturer assesses itself, but for listed categories a notified body must take part. The route is fixed before release, so the evidence the manifest keeps must be evidence an outside assessor can open.

The map also fixes how far this book's own vocabulary reaches. The verdicts, the release manifest, and the signed capability limits are this book's architecture for carrying a decision into the running machine, not requirements of any standard above. A standard asks for a documented argument, a rated safety function, and an assessment. The architecture is one way to keep that argument tied to the machine after the assessment ends.

## The Three Verdicts {#sec-release-three-verdicts}

Every row of @tbl-16-cae-scorecard ends in an adjudication, and the release decision resolves the whole assertion DAG into one of three verdicts: **unconditional operation**\index{Verdicts!unconditional operation}, **conditional operation**\index{Verdicts!conditional operation}, or **refusal to operate**\index{Verdicts!refusal to operate}. In this book's architecture, these verdicts are not informal administrative labels or advisory certificates; they are signed capability descriptors loaded into the real-time safety microcontroller before motor power stages are energized. No standard requires that mechanism (@sec-release-standards-map); it is one way to make the verdict govern the running machine. The first verdict, unconditional operation (`UNCOND`), authorizes tracking proposals across the full operating envelope named in a signed release manifest while its standing conditions remain verified. Each hazard claim in that case requires empirical evidence for the specified physical plant, payload distribution, operational design domain, and fault set. Brake thermal capacity, stopping clearance, and tracking-error bounds must be qualified for that envelope (@sec-body-thermal-duty-cycles), and independent permission checks must stand wherever learned proposals can reach actuators (@sec-boundary-causal-boundary). The verdict does not eliminate residual or newly discovered hazards; it authorizes operation only under the assessed claims and requires detection and withdrawal within the qualified response budget when a physical premise fails.

### Authorization boundaries and access restrictions {#sec-release-verdicts-ssm}

The second verdict, conditional operation (`COND`), applies when empirical evidence supports the stated hazard claims within a restricted operating subset but lacks valid warrants for the full envelope. In the running machine, `COND` selects a pre-validated safety configuration, in the way safety controllers and protective scanners switch between validated field sets[^fn-scanner-field-sets] and speed-monitoring cases. Its restricted kinematic thresholds ($v_{\max} \le v_{\text{restricted}}$, $a_{\max} \le a_{\text{restricted}}$) and spatial geofences were assessed as a configuration before release; the verdict selects them and never writes arbitrary parameters. The signing and loading mechanics are collected in @sec-appendix-systems-release-protocol. Whereas a conditional verdict (`COND`) is an offline, predeployment contract that restricts the machine's operating envelope until re-adjudication, a degraded mode is an online runtime fallback invoked when an active subsystem experiences transient loss of telemetry or sensor redundancy. Release then enforces physical, kinematic, or environmental boundaries that exclude unverified hazard states, such as de-rated joint velocities, a restricted illumination range, or a physical barrier that keeps humans outside the manipulator's workspace. Where contact force cannot be bounded for unseparated co-presence, a restricted case may require an assessed physical cell and validated access interlocks (@fig-16-real-robot-safety-cell), verified so the protective stop completes before a human can breach the hazardous volume.

[^fn-scanner-field-sets]: **Safety Scanner Field Sets**\index{Safety laser scanner!field sets}: A safety laser scanner stores several protective-field geometries that were configured and validated in advance, and a safety controller selects one of them from encoded speed or position inputs. The scanner never computes a new field at runtime. `COND` borrows the pattern, so the verdict selects a pre-assessed limit set and no untested parameter can reach the permission path.

::: {#fig-16-real-robot-safety-cell fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Physical separation example**: A yellow industrial arm works behind yellow mesh fencing. Fencing can be one condition of a restricted release when a validated access interlock and stopping test support it. (Photo: PEO ACWA, Pueblo Chemical Agent-Destruction Pilot Plant, 2012, [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Pueblo_Chemical_Agent-Destruction_Pilot_Plant_Robotic_Operating_Area_(8456400290).jpg), [CC BY 2.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/2.0/).)" fig-alt="Yellow industrial robot arm and metal equipment inside a factory bay bounded by yellow mesh fence panels and gates. A blue lift is outside the foreground fence. Wiring, interlock rating, and stopping behavior are not visible."}
![](images/jpg/fig16_real_robot_safety_cell.jpg){width="85%" fig-alt="Yellow industrial robot arm and metal equipment inside a factory bay bounded by yellow mesh fence panels and gates. A blue lift is outside the foreground fence. Wiring, interlock rating, and stopping behavior are not visible."}
:::

Dynamic speed and separation monitoring would require a different access claim from the stationary-person case used here. Its clearance must include human approach throughout reaction and stopping, robot travel before response onset, the executed stopping profile, and uncertainty. The warehouse case retains its controlled crossing rule; it cannot replace that rule with a stationary-person stopping calculation and call the result open-floor collaboration.

Every quantitative condition attached to a release verdict names the operational limit the permission path enforces, with margin below the calculated physical ceiling. The item handover shows the difference. The contract signs a Tool Center Point (TCP)\index{Tool Center Point!handover speed contract} speed below the ceiling that the contact criterion admits under @eq-release-unbraked-force, and the gap between the two speeds is the allowance for what the monitor cannot see at the instant it samples: speed growth between samples, encoder quantization error, and the drive's response to an enforcement clamp. A contract signed at the ceiling leaves no room for those terms, and the release case needs a measured bound on each before the signed speed can stand.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Deterministic fallback coverage supporting conditional release verdicts builds on @sec-enforcement-fallback-ladder.
:::

The inspected-floor condition follows the same rule. Where the site's inspection regime certifies a friction coefficient of only `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.mu_inspected_str`, the credible deceleration falls to what that friction supports, and the budget that admits `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.v_ceiling_str` on surveyed floors admits only `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.v_inspected_ceiling_str`. A visual inspection alone cannot establish this lower friction bound: transparent oil remains below it. The site must qualify the friction assessment and the cleaning, spill-isolation, and access procedures that preserve the assessed floor state between checks. If that regime cannot exclude the film over the authorized interval, reduced speed does not rescue the case; the aisle remains refused.

The third verdict, refusal to operate (`REFUSE`), is the mandatory outcome whenever the safety case contains missing warrants, uncharacterized tail latencies, incomplete fault-injection coverage, or unmonitored failure modes. For systems where torque removal causes harm (such as upright bipedal humanoids falling under gravity), `REFUSE` cannot simply drop motor currents to zero; it must mandate an assessed, powered descent or seated hold. If the enforcer's worst-case execution time under the placement's load has never been measured against its `{python} ReleaseClaims.deadline_str` deadline, or the fault set omitted the common-cause tests the placement names, the hazard remains unquantified and cannot support release. Refusal is likewise required when a physical measurement contradicts the model behind a budget term, such as loaded stopping trials that decelerate below the `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.a_brake_str` the budget assumes.

A refusal verdict is an engineering deliverable, not an administrative failure. It moves a dispute between schedule and safety onto evidence by isolating the broken link in the assertion DAG. If release is refused because loaded stopping trials contradict the braking term, the team does not debate risk tolerance but repeats the trials at the loaded mass until the low tail of the deceleration is known, re-derives the stopping term from that tail, and returns for re-adjudication only when the aisle budget closes on the measured value. The refusal verdict defines the exact evidentiary test that must pass before re-adjudication can occur.

Accountability for the release decision must reside with an identifiable **lead systems adjudicator**\index{Lead systems adjudicator!accountability} rather than being diffused across development teams. When a vision team signs off on detection scores, an actuator supplier on torque curves, and a learning team on policy convergence, each assumes that another layer provides the margin. The adjudicator alone attests that the integrated system satisfies the safety case, and the attestation binds the verdict to a set of immutable technical artifacts, including the cryptographic hash of the verified policy weights, the calibration logs of the arm's contact-force sensing, the brake-onset trials together with a separately justified worst-response bound, and the stopping trials at the loaded mass that establish the credible deceleration. The adjudicator signs the release manifest with a private key held in a hardware security module,[^fn-hsm-release-signing] committing personal and institutional accountability to the integrity of the evidence; the machine verifies that signature against a public key anchored in its own hardware root of trust.

[^fn-hsm-release-signing]: **Hardware Security Module (HSM)**\index{Hardware security module!release signing}: A tamper-resistant device generates and stores private keys and performs signing inside its own boundary, so the key never leaves it. A signature from the HSM therefore identifies which accountable key holder approved a manifest, not merely someone who obtained a copy of a key file.

The adjudicator's signature is the developer's own acceptance, and external acceptance is a separate act. UL 4600 calls for independent assessment of the safety case [@ul4600], and a machine whose safety functions rely on machine learning falls, under the Machinery Regulation, among the products that need a third-party conformity assessment (@sec-release-standards-map). Independence matters for the same reason diverse legs do in an argument. An assessor who did not build the case does not share the assumptions that shaped its evidence, and so can find the premise the developer's own review was organized not to see. The release manifest must therefore preserve the raw evidence an assessor needs, not only the verdict it supported.

The adjudicator signs one of the three decisions in @tbl-16-verdicts-taxonomy. A conditional verdict needs a separately evidenced restricted envelope; a known hole in the nominal argument cannot simply be relabeled as a safe restriction. No verdict moves the proposal boundary. Under `UNCOND` and `COND` alike the policy only proposes and the enforcer still admits each action, as principle \ref{pri-vol4-proposal-permission} requires, so a release sets the envelope the permission path enforces and never grants the policy permission of its own.

| Signed verdict | Evidence required                                                                                                | Permission and runtime limits                                                                                                                                          | Expiry or refusal trigger                                       |
|:---------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------|
| `UNCOND`       | Full operating-envelope claim, measured plant and timing bounds, independently validated permission and fallback | Policy proposes across full *signed* task envelope; every action passes the enforcer                                                                                   | Evidence, configuration, calibration, or standing premise fails |
| `COND`         | Restricted operating-envelope claim and its own evidence, limits, and fault coverage                             | Policy proposes only within signed reduced limits; every action passes the enforcer                                                                                    | Any restricted premise becomes false or unknown                 |
| `REFUSE`       | Missing, contradictory, expired, or unauthenticated critical evidence                                            | No autonomous tracking permit; execute the assessed stop or hold, the fallback-ladder rung the release case validates for the plant (@sec-enforcement-fallback-ladder) | Re-adjudication with repaired evidence                          |

: **Three signed release verdicts for the mobile manipulator**: Full operation and restricted mode both retain independent per-action permission. Refusal is an actionable engineering result. {#tbl-16-verdicts-taxonomy tbl-colwidths="[14,32,32,22]"}

Each verdict is signed against the machine as it was measured. The body behind those measurements keeps changing after the signature, so a verdict lasts only as long as the conditions that keep checking it.

## The Verdict's Standing Conditions {#sec-release-standing-conditions}

A signed release can lapse without any change to its software. A brake lining wears, a camera bracket shifts, or a lane is polished by traffic, and the stopping claim the adjudicator signed no longer holds. Standing conditions keep the release tied to such physical premises by specifying when each is checked and what happens when it fails. Their observation schedules follow the failure mechanism rather than the software release cycle. A case maintained this way, updated through the operating life as monitored evidence changes, is what the assurance literature calls a *dynamic safety case*\index{Safety case!dynamic} [@denney2015dynamic].

### Mechanical degradation and thermal calibration drift {#sec-release-calibration-drift}

None of the three verdicts is a permanent grant. Mechanical linkages develop backlash, friction surfaces wear, lenses accumulate dust, and ambient distributions change, so operating under `UNCOND` or `COND` carries obligations for the life of the deployment. Brake wear that lowers the loaded deceleration by the shortfall that spends the aisle budget's spare (@sec-release-question) leaves the budget no allowance for any other input error. That wear must fail a standing condition (a scheduled stopping trial or a validated brake self-test) before the machine re-enters the aisle, since a stop in service would first reveal it at a rack end. Each such obligation pairs a premise with a detector and a response, which makes it one of the standing conditions the verdict carries.

Sensor mounting drift can invalidate localization while images remain fresh. Thermal expansion and vibration alter the measured geometry, and software rollback cannot restore a displaced bracket. The case therefore needs a qualified drift check or scheduled physical inspection and recalibration, with an interval justified by the observed mechanism. A checksum protects the stored calibration record; it cannot establish that the sensor still occupies the recorded pose.

### The envelope trichotomy and epistemic gaps {#sec-release-envelope-trichotomy-sub}

```{python}
#| label: calc-release-standing-premises
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ STANDING PREMISES OF THE MACHINE'S RELEASE
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-release-standing-conditions (opening paragraph and the
# │          envelope-membership paragraph).
# │ Goal: Tie the standing conditions to the premises the machine's claims use.
# │ Show: friction needed for a_brake against dry concrete, tote-rack capacity,
# │       and the base tracking bound.
# │ How: RM/AISLE fields; mu_min = a_brake / g. The permission rail's hold-up
# │      is sized in @sec-enforcement-fallback-ladder; the manifest only signs it.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, fmt_mass, fmt_length, check

# ┌── 1. LOAD: the running machine and its site ─────────────────────────────────
RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator  # category: illustrative (running machine)
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle  # category: illustrative (aisle scene; speeds, lease, and tick chosen)
g_std = (1 * ureg.standard_gravity).to(meter / second**2)  # category: datasheet (standard gravity, a defined physical constant; Pint)

# ┌── 2. EXECUTE ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
mu_min = (AISLE.a_brake / g_std).to("dimensionless").magnitude

# ┌── 3. GUARD ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
check(abs(mu_min - 0.204) < 5e-4, "Friction floor 0.204")
check(mu_min < AISLE.mu_dry, "Dry concrete exceeds the friction floor")
check(abs(RM.onboard_payload_capacity.to(kilogram).magnitude - 50.0) < 1e-9, "Tote-rack capacity 50 kg")
check(abs(AISLE.eps_track.to(millimeter).magnitude - 40.0) < 1e-9, "Tracking bound 40 mm")

# ┌── 4. OUTPUT ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
class ReleaseStandingPremises:
    mu_min_str = fmt(round(mu_min, 3), precision=3)
    mu_dry_str = fmt(AISLE.mu_dry, precision=2)
    payload_str = fmt_mass(RM.onboard_payload_capacity, unit=kilogram, precision=0)
    eps_track_str = fmt_length(AISLE.eps_track, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
```

A release verdict depends on physical premises with different observation schedules. The mobile manipulator's braking claim relies on floor friction of at least `{python} ReleaseStandingPremises.mu_min_str`, which dry concrete at about `{python} ReleaseStandingPremises.mu_dry_str` exceeds, but a one-time survey cannot cover spills or surface wear. The case needs a floor inspection schedule and a stop or exclusion rule after contamination, with any on-board traction monitor specified separately. The arm's contact-force calibration is re-established at a documented interval. Each premise must remain valid at the cadence required by its physical failure mode. Under principle \ref{pri-vol4-evidence-bounds-authority}, the verdict grants authority per operating condition, and that authority lasts only while the evidence behind each premise stays current.

Every runtime-monitored premise requires a detector and a pre-allocated response; premises maintained by site procedures require an accountable owner and an enforceable stop or exclusion rule. If the case charges a navigation-camera dispatch age of `{python} ReleaseClaims.t_age_str`, it must measure that age at dispatch and account for subsequent processing and execution separately. A copied dispatch-age field cannot establish current evidence age. Without the event-referenced timestamp checks, the premise has not been monitored. It has silently degraded into an assumption. The tote-rack load, bounded by its `{python} ReleaseStandingPremises.payload_str` capacity, changes only when the arm places or removes a tote, so a check at each pick suffices, while speed and lease validity are checked on every `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.t_tick_str` permission tick.

Evaluating monitored premises at runtime exposes a trichotomy in **envelope membership**\index{Envelope membership!trichotomy states} (\ref{dfn-release-envelope-trichotomy}). A binary check presumes normal execution whenever no fault flag is set, but envelope membership has three states: known-true, known-false, and unknown. Membership is known-true when verified telemetry and event-referenced timestamps support a qualified uncertainty set that remains inside the admissible physical bounds. Estimator convergence or finite covariance alone does not establish that containment. When a physical limit is breached, such as base tracking error exceeding the `{python} ReleaseStandingPremises.eps_track_str` bound that the stopping envelope insets, the state is known-false. When an optical encoder drops communication, a camera frame arrives with a cyclic redundancy check (CRC) mismatch, or an extended Kalman filter diverges, the machine enters an epistemic gap where it cannot determine whether it is inside or outside its signed operating envelope.

When the evidence supporting active motion becomes unknown or false, the enforcer revokes tracking and selects the validated response for the current plant state. This is different from refusing an invalid replacement proposal: an already admitted chunk can continue only while its own evidence, state bounds, and lease remain valid. Diagnostic records preserve whether the cause was missing evidence or an observed violation, while the response preserves the energy and sensing needed to stop or hold.

::: {#dfn-release-envelope-trichotomy .callout-definition title="Envelope trichotomy"}

![](images/svg/dfn_envelope_trichotomy.svg){fig-alt="Three boxes left to right: known-true with a qualified uncertainty set inside the envelope and fresh verified evidence; unknown, reached when evidence is lost, from dropout, CRC mismatch, or estimator divergence; and known-false, reached over the top when a boundary breach is measured, such as tracking error above its bound. A bracket under known-true reads permit equals 1, tracking may continue. One bracket under unknown and known-false reads permit equals 0, validated stop or hold, logged causes stay distinct." width=100%}

***Envelope trichotomy***\index{Envelope trichotomy!definition}\index{Operating envelope!trichotomy} is the three-state epistemic classification of cyber-physical system health relative to its signed operating envelope: *known-true* (qualified state-uncertainty set contained inside the supported envelope), *known-false* (verified boundary violation triggering deterministic hardware refusal), and *unknown* (epistemic state uncertainty due to sensor dropout, frame corruption, or estimator divergence).

1.  **Significance**: An unknown state is not evidence of a boundary breach, but neither supports continued tracking. The permission decision is refusal in both unknown and known-false states; the logged cause remains distinct and the response depends on the plant's validated stop or hold capability.
2.  **Distinction**: Unlike a binary boolean status check (`is_safe == true`), the envelope trichotomy isolates epistemic blindness from active violations, ensuring telemetry loss is never mistaken for safe clearance.
3.  **Common pitfall**: Treating a stored command as indefinitely valid after communication fails. An active chunk may continue only within its own still-valid evidence and lease; otherwise the assessed fallback must take over.

:::

The same three states govern the evidence behind each premise. A trial marked `UNOBSERVABLE` or `INVALID` in @sec-verification-oracles-acceptance supplies no evidence, so the premise it was meant to test stays unknown, and an unknown premise refuses the claim that depends on it; only `PASS` records count toward a verdict, and a `FAIL` record makes the premise known-false.

### Blind travel, kinetic consequences, and cycle limits {#sec-release-blind-travel-limits}

The consequence of a sensor or communication blackout depends on speed, clearance, contact geometry, and the response the plant can still execute. When telemetry fails, the machine must execute a deterministic fallback before kinetic displacement breaches clearance boundaries.

```{python}
#| label: calc-release-blind-travel
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ BLIND TRAVEL AND THE FALLBACK RESPONSE
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-release-standing-conditions (fallback-response paragraph and
# │          the enforcement-path paragraph after it).
# │ Goal: Size the consequence of continuing without telemetry on the machine.
# │ Show: loaded kinetic energy at aisle speed, travel per millisecond, the
# │       degraded-mode speed, the permission tick, renewal-to-onset time, and
# │       the response to a premise the enforcer monitors itself.
# │ How: calc_kinetic_energy with RM.loaded_mass and AISLE.v_aisle.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_energy, fmt_mass, fmt_length, fmt_velocity, fmt_latency, check
from mlsysim.physics.robotics import calc_kinetic_energy

# ┌── 1. LOAD: the running machine, plus one chapter-local input ────────────────
RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator  # category: illustrative (running machine)
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle  # category: illustrative (aisle scene; speeds, lease, and tick chosen)
degraded_fraction = 0.5  # category: chosen (degraded mode halves the aisle speed)

# ┌── 2. EXECUTE ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
e_k_loaded = calc_kinetic_energy(RM.loaded_mass, AISLE.v_aisle).to(joule)
travel_per_ms = (AISLE.v_aisle * (1 * millisecond)).to(millimeter)
v_degraded = (degraded_fraction * AISLE.v_aisle).to(meter / second)
t_renewal_to_onset = (AISLE.t_lease + AISLE.t_tick + AISLE.t_bus + AISLE.t_brake_onset).to(millisecond)
t_monitor_response = (AISLE.t_tick + AISLE.t_bus + AISLE.t_brake_onset).to(millisecond)  # enforcer-detected premise

# ┌── 3. GUARD ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
check(abs(e_k_loaded.magnitude - 310.96) < 0.01, "Loaded kinetic energy at 1.3 m/s")
check(abs(travel_per_ms.magnitude - 1.3) < 1e-9, "1.3 mm of travel per millisecond")
check(abs(v_degraded.magnitude - 0.65) < 1e-9, "Degraded mode at 0.65 m/s")
check(abs(t_renewal_to_onset.magnitude - 82.0) < 1e-9, "Renewal to brake onset 82 ms")
check(abs(t_monitor_response.magnitude - 22.0) < 1e-9, "Enforcer tick + bus + brake onset 22 ms")
# margin_silent_proposer_response_strip.svg fig-alt hand-types the lease and each window
check(abs(AISLE.t_lease.to(millisecond).magnitude - 60.0) < 1e-9, "Chunk lease 60 ms")
check(abs(AISLE.t_bus.to(millisecond).magnitude - 1.0) < 1e-9, "Bus transfer 1 ms")
check(abs(AISLE.t_brake_onset.to(millisecond).magnitude - 20.0) < 1e-9, "Brake onset 20 ms")

# ┌── 4. OUTPUT ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
class ReleaseBlindTravel:
    m1_str = fmt_mass(RM.loaded_mass, unit=kilogram, precision=0)
    v_aisle_str = fmt_velocity(AISLE.v_aisle, unit=meter / second, precision=1)
    e_k_str = fmt_energy(round(e_k_loaded.magnitude) * joule, unit=joule, precision=0)
    travel_per_ms_str = fmt_length(travel_per_ms, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    v_degraded_str = fmt_velocity(v_degraded, unit=meter / second, precision=2)
    t_tick_str = fmt_latency(AISLE.t_tick, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_renewal_to_onset_str = fmt_latency(t_renewal_to_onset, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_monitor_response_str = fmt_latency(t_monitor_response, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_lease_str = fmt_latency(AISLE.t_lease, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    # Response windows for the margin strip (generator reads the quantities)
    t_lease = AISLE.t_lease.to(millisecond)
    t_tick = AISLE.t_tick.to(millisecond)
    t_bus = AISLE.t_bus.to(millisecond)
    t_onset = AISLE.t_brake_onset.to(millisecond)
    t_silent = t_renewal_to_onset
    t_monitored = t_monitor_response
```

The response to an unevaluable premise follows from the physical consequence of continuing motion without telemetry, not from a severity label. When the mobile manipulator runs the aisle at `{python} ReleaseBlindTravel.v_aisle_str` with its tote rack full, its `{python} ReleaseBlindTravel.m1_str` loaded mass carries `{python} ReleaseBlindTravel.e_k_str` of kinetic energy. If its lidar stops transmitting updates, each millisecond of blind travel carries the machine `{python} ReleaseBlindTravel.travel_per_ms_str` closer to an unmapped obstacle. The safety case fixes three responses in advance. Two of them exist only where the signed case covers them: a **degraded mode**\index{Degraded mode!velocity reduction} that continues when redundant sensors still bound positional uncertainty, such as reducing the aisle speed to `{python} ReleaseBlindTravel.v_degraded_str` while a qualified redundant observation path still covers obstacles, and the restricted mode of a `COND` verdict\index{Release verdict!conditional} that clamps torque or confines proposals to a precomputed corridor. Wheel odometry alone cannot establish fresh obstacle clearance. The third, the STOP response (@sec-enforcement-fallback-ladder)\index{Fallback ladder!STOP rung}, requires its own fault coverage and uses the configured drive and brake sequence when observability is lost; its ability to stop within clearance depends on the current speed, response delay, and measured braking capability.

The action lease bounds how long an admitted chunk can execute without renewal. It is not renewed by asserting that every environmental premise has been remeasured on each tick. The permission path checks current local evidence and the signed validity of slower site and maintenance records. A proposer delay becomes lost service only while that path and its fallback remain independent and valid.

Standing conditions that affect motion need an enforcement path with a measured detection and response budget. In the architecture of @sec-enforcement, the independent enforcer\index{Safety enforcer!hardware interlock} checks proposals and monitored premises before issuing actuator permission. The machine's permission path decides on a `{python} ReleaseBlindTravel.t_tick_str` tick. Its `{python} ReleaseBlindTravel.t_renewal_to_onset_str` bound from the last valid renewal to brake onset covers a proposer that stops renewing. Once a failure flag is locally available to the enforcer, the tick, bus transfer, and physical response onset contribute `{python} ReleaseBlindTravel.t_monitor_response_str` in the illustrative budget. Any delay from the physical failure to that flag is additional and must be qualified; the local response subtotal cannot stand for the full detection-to-stop chain. When a premise is unknown or false, the enforcer revokes tracking and commands the rung of the fallback ladder that suits the plant's state (@sec-enforcement-fallback-ladder), and the signed release case must include that stop choice and its measured timing.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/margin_silent_proposer_response_strip.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Two horizontal timelines in milliseconds. Silent proposer: a 60-millisecond lease, 2 milliseconds of tick and bus transfer, and 20 milliseconds of brake onset, 82 milliseconds in total. Monitored premise: the same 2 milliseconds and 20 milliseconds, 22 milliseconds in total."}

*A silent proposer is stopped only after its `{python} ReleaseBlindTravel.t_lease_str` lease runs out; a watched premise, within `{python} ReleaseBlindTravel.t_monitor_response_str`.*
:::

The selected base response uses powered deceleration before setting holding brakes at rest. Logic and brake-coil hold-up do not supply drive torque: the release case must establish drive energy, sensing, and actuation continuity for every fault credited with this stop. Torque inhibit is a distinct response and inherits no stopping-distance budget from the powered sequence.

The transition into an unknown or known-false state also triggers local evidence capture. The trace must preserve the observations preceding refusal and the actual fallback response, even if the same fault interrupts the network or main power. That record supports later adjudication; it cannot delay the live response. The capture and review path is developed in @sec-release-data-curation-flywheel.

On longer timescales, even when every runtime heartbeat succeeds, the **release verdict**\index{Release verdict!invalidation} carries an operational cycle and inspection budget.[^fn-rule-fatigue-derating] Operating hours and mechanical fatigue degrade physical components in ways that high-frequency telemetry cannot observe directly (such as surface pitting on gear teeth, elastomer seal stiffening, or fastener preload relaxation). Once this cycle budget expires, the release case must be re-adjudicated before further autonomous motion is permitted.

[^fn-rule-fatigue-derating]: **Mechanical Fatigue Budget**\index{Fatigue limits!cyclic derating}: A cumulative-damage model such as Miner's rule ($\sum_i n_i/N_i$) [@miner1945cumulative] can organize a measured load spectrum against component-specific fatigue data; it is an approximation, not a universal failure deadline. The assessed loads, uncertainty, inspection evidence, and stopping consequences determine any signed payload derating and cycle limit. An expired limit revokes the applicable release case rather than silently extending service.

A verdict therefore stands only while each of its standing conditions is known-true, checked at the cadence its failure mode sets and backed by a response whose timing the case has measured. With claims, verdicts, and the conditions that revoke them defined, the adjudicator can take the mobile manipulator's six claims one at a time and decide its release on the evidence this book holds.

## End-to-End Safety Case Demonstration {#sec-release-case-worked-full}

Adjudicating the release case requires evaluating each physical warrant against available empirical traces. When applied to the warehouse mobile manipulator across its six core claims, this adjudication process isolates the exact boundary where mathematical deduction ends and empirical measurement must begin.

```{python}
#| label: calc-release-worked-verdict
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ ADJUDICATING THE MACHINE'S RELEASE
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-release-case-worked-full (the door branch cites
# │          @eq-release-trip-indentation and @eq-release-coupled-indentation,
# │          derived in @sec-enforcement-intentional-contact), and
# │          @tbl-16-cond-measurements.
# │ Goal: Show that each claim's warrant rests on a premise the book's evidence
# │       leaves illustrative, and list the measurements that would move it.
# │ Show: latch force at brake command and the arm stop it requires at the
# │       guarded and unsupported approaches; the base budget and spare; the
# │       illustrative value behind each premise; the handover force; the
# │       restricted aisle speed a COND case could sign.
# │ How: latch and handover premises from EnforcementContactForce
# │      (calc-release-contact-premises); the budget
# │      and ceilings from the jerk-limited S-curve stop (calc_scurve_stop_distance,
# │      calc_scurve_max_permitted_velocity; jerk bound = the reference C2
# │      polynomial's peak jerk at the drive limit).
# │ Note:    Reads v_restricted from ReleaseEnvelope (calc-release-operating-
# │          envelope), so the chosen restricted speed is set in one place.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, fmt_int, fmt_force, fmt_sci_qty, fmt_latency, fmt_acceleration, fmt_length, fmt_velocity, check
from mlsysim.physics.robotics import (
    calc_c2_stop_suffix,
    calc_scurve_stop_distance,
    calc_scurve_max_permitted_velocity,
)

# ┌── 1. LOAD: the running machine and its site ─────────────────────────────────
RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator  # category: illustrative (running machine)
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle  # category: illustrative (aisle scene; speeds, lease, and tick chosen)
g_std = (1 * ureg.standard_gravity).to(meter / second**2)  # category: datasheet (standard gravity, a defined physical constant; Pint)
v_restricted = ReleaseEnvelope.v_restricted  # chosen; set once in calc-release-operating-envelope

# ┌── 2. EXECUTE: the door branch, then the base spare ──────────────────────────
# Door branch: premises from the enforcement record (calc-release-contact-premises).
f_cmd_lo = EnforcementContactForce.f_cmd
x_rem_lo = EnforcementContactForce.x_rem
a_arm_lo = EnforcementContactForce.a_arm
t_arm_stop = EnforcementContactForce.t_arm_stop
f_cmd_hi = EnforcementContactForce.f_cmd_hi
a_arm_hi = EnforcementContactForce.a_arm_hi

overhead_loc = AISLE.delta_loc + AISLE.eps_track
# Jerk bound: the reference C2 polynomial's peak jerk at the drive limit (@sec-planning-c2-stopping-suffix)
j_brake = calc_c2_stop_suffix(RM.base.max_velocity, AISLE.a_brake)["peak_jerk"].to(meter / second**3)
budget_aisle = (
    AISLE.v_aisle * AISLE.tau_delay + calc_scurve_stop_distance(AISLE.v_aisle, AISLE.a_brake, j_brake) + overhead_loc + AISLE.delta_margin
).to(millimeter)
spare_aisle = (AISLE.d_clear - budget_aisle).to(millimeter)
mu_min = (AISLE.a_brake / g_std).to("dimensionless").magnitude
# The floor caps the deceleration; the jerk bound belongs to the load and is unchanged.
a_inspected = min(AISLE.a_brake, (AISLE.mu_inspected_floor * g_std).to(meter / second**2))
v_inspected_ceiling = calc_scurve_max_permitted_velocity(AISLE.d_clear, AISLE.tau_delay, a_inspected, j_brake, overhead_loc, AISLE.delta_margin).to(
    meter / second
)
v_ceiling = calc_scurve_max_permitted_velocity(AISLE.d_clear, AISLE.tau_delay, AISLE.a_brake, j_brake, overhead_loc, AISLE.delta_margin).to(
    meter / second
)
t_renewal_to_onset = (AISLE.t_lease + AISLE.t_tick + AISLE.t_bus + AISLE.t_brake_onset).to(millisecond)
f_handover = EnforcementContactForce.f_handover

# ┌── 3. GUARD: canon values quoted in the prose and the table ──────────────────
check(abs(f_cmd_lo.magnitude - 39.0) < 1e-9, "Latch force at brake command, guarded approach")
check(abs(x_rem_lo.magnitude - 0.1525) < 1e-6, "Remaining compression 0.15 mm")
check(abs(a_arm_lo.magnitude - 2.95) < 0.005, "Arm stop premise about 3 m/s^2 (computed 2.95)")
check(abs(t_arm_stop.magnitude - 10.0) < 0.5, "Arm stop takes about 10 ms")
check(abs(f_cmd_hi.magnitude - 95.0) < 1e-9, "Latch force at brake command, unsupported approach")
check(abs(a_arm_hi.magnitude - 400.0) < 1e-6, "Unsupported approach needs 400 m/s^2")
check(abs(spare_aisle.magnitude - 131.0075) < 5e-3, "Spare at 1.3 m/s")
check(abs(mu_min - 0.204) < 5e-4, "Friction floor 0.204")
check(abs(v_inspected_ceiling.magnitude - 1.2309) < 5e-5, "Inspected-floor ceiling 1.23 m/s")
check(abs(v_ceiling.magnitude - 1.4367) < 5e-5, "Aisle ceiling 1.44 m/s")
check(abs(t_renewal_to_onset.magnitude - 82.0) < 1e-9, "Renewal to brake onset 82 ms")
check(RM.chunk_inference_latency < AISLE.t_lease, "Chunk inference fits inside the lease")
check(abs(f_handover.magnitude - 20.70) < 0.01, "Transient handover force 20.7 N")
check(v_restricted < v_inspected_ceiling < AISLE.v_aisle, "Restricted mode sits below the inspected-floor ceiling")
a_arm_ratio = (a_arm_hi / a_arm_lo).to("dimensionless").magnitude
# margin_arm_stop_demand_ladder.svg fig-alt hand-types 3, 9.8 and 400 m/s^2; caption says over a hundredfold
check(abs(a_arm_ratio - 135.6) < 0.1, "The unsupported approach needs about 136 times the guarded arm stop")
check(abs(g_std.magnitude - 9.80665) < 1e-9, "Standard gravity 9.8 m/s^2")

# ┌── 4. OUTPUT: rendered values ────────────────────────────────────────────────
class ReleaseWorkedVerdict:
    # Door branch of C1
    v_latch_str = fmt_velocity(AISLE.v_latch_approach, unit=meter / second, precision=2)
    k_latch_str = fmt_sci_qty(AISLE.k_latch, newton / meter, precision=1)
    f_trip_str = fmt_force(AISLE.f_latch_tripwire, precision=0)
    t_contact_str = fmt_latency(AISLE.t_contact_response, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    f_cmd_str = fmt_force(f_cmd_lo, precision=0)
    f_latch_limit_str = fmt_force(AISLE.f_latch_limit, precision=0)
    x_remaining_str = fmt_length(round(x_rem_lo.magnitude, 2) * millimeter, unit=millimeter, precision=2)
    a_arm_str = fmt_acceleration(round(a_arm_lo.magnitude) * meter / second**2, unit=meter / second**2, precision=0)
    t_arm_stop_str = fmt_latency(round(t_arm_stop.magnitude) * millisecond, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    v_latch_high_str = fmt_velocity(AISLE.v_latch_high, unit=meter / second, precision=2)
    f_cmd_high_str = fmt_force(f_cmd_hi, precision=0)
    a_arm_high_str = fmt_acceleration(a_arm_hi, unit=meter / second**2, precision=0)
    # Other branches
    budget_str = fmt_length(budget_aisle, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    spare_str = fmt_length(spare_aisle, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    wcet_str = fmt_latency(AISLE.enforcer_wcet, unit=microsecond, precision=0)
    enforcer_unloaded_str = fmt_latency(AISLE.enforcer_unloaded, unit=microsecond, precision=0)
    deadline_str = fmt_latency(AISLE.enforcer_deadline, unit=microsecond, precision=0)
    t_age_str = fmt_latency(AISLE.perception_age, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    mu_min_str = fmt(round(mu_min, 3), precision=3)
    # Measurement table: the illustrative value behind each premise
    a_brake_str = fmt_acceleration(AISLE.a_brake, unit=meter / second**2, precision=0)
    v_ceiling_str = fmt_velocity(round(v_ceiling.magnitude, 2) * meter / second, unit=meter / second, precision=2)
    t_act_str = fmt_latency(AISLE.t_brake_onset, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_renewal_to_onset_str = fmt_latency(t_renewal_to_onset, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    eps_track_str = fmt_length(AISLE.eps_track, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
    delta_loc_str = fmt_length(AISLE.delta_loc, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
    d_clear_str = fmt_length(AISLE.d_clear, unit=meter, precision=2)
    mu_dry_str = fmt(AISLE.mu_dry, precision=2)
    v_inspected_ceiling_str = fmt_velocity(round(v_inspected_ceiling.magnitude, 2) * meter / second, unit=meter / second, precision=2)
    t_chunk_str = fmt_latency(RM.chunk_inference_latency, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_lease_str = fmt_latency(AISLE.t_lease, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    v_handover_str = fmt_velocity(AISLE.v_handover, unit=meter / second, precision=2)
    f_handover_str = fmt_force(f_handover, precision=1)
    v_restricted_str = fmt_velocity(v_restricted, unit=meter / second, precision=0)
    v_aisle_str = fmt_velocity(AISLE.v_aisle, unit=meter / second, precision=1)
    a_arm_ratio_str = fmt_int(round(a_arm_ratio))
    # Arm-stop demands for the margin ladder (generator reads the quantities)
    a_arm_lo = a_arm_lo
    a_arm_hi = a_arm_hi
    g = g_std
    v_latch = AISLE.v_latch_approach
    v_latch_high = AISLE.v_latch_high
```

The adjudicator takes each of the six claims in @tbl-16-cae-scorecard, finds the premise that carries its warrant, and asks what kind of number supports that premise. The door branch of C1 shows the procedure in full.

The enforcement record supplies the door branch's arithmetic (@sec-enforcement-intentional-contact), and the adjudicator takes it as stated. At the guarded approach of `{python} ReleaseWorkedVerdict.v_latch_str`, @eq-release-trip-indentation puts the force at physical braking onset at `{python} ReleaseWorkedVerdict.f_cmd_str`, well inside the `{python} ReleaseWorkedVerdict.f_latch_limit_str` latch limit, and @eq-release-coupled-indentation leaves the plate only `{python} ReleaseWorkedVerdict.x_remaining_str` of further compression, within which the arm must stop at about `{python} ReleaseWorkedVerdict.a_arm_str`, an illustrative stop of about `{python} ReleaseWorkedVerdict.t_arm_stop_str`. At the unsupported `{python} ReleaseWorkedVerdict.v_latch_high_str`, the force at onset is already `{python} ReleaseWorkedVerdict.f_cmd_high_str`, and the stop would need `{python} ReleaseWorkedVerdict.a_arm_high_str`. The calculation identifies the stopping capability that a release claim would have to establish; it does not provide evidence that the arm can achieve it. The operating envelope (@tbl-16-odd-invariants) therefore excludes this approach. Increasing approach speed tightens the contact stopping requirement (@sec-training-contact-exploit), while the available demonstration distribution supplies no evidence for the faster contact (@sec-data-failure-modes).

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/margin_arm_stop_demand_ladder.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Log-scale ladder of three horizontal bars for the arm deceleration needed to stop inside the latch: 400 meters per second squared at a 0.10 meters per second approach, a gray reference bar for 1 g at 9.8, and 3 meters per second squared at the guarded 0.03 meters per second approach."}

*Raising the approach from `{python} ReleaseWorkedVerdict.v_latch_str` to `{python} ReleaseWorkedVerdict.v_latch_high_str` multiplies the arm stop needed `{python} ReleaseWorkedVerdict.a_arm_ratio_str`-fold.*
:::

Neither result is in doubt as arithmetic: the algebraic deduction is exact. However, engineering authorization cannot rest on closed-form mathematics alone. The door branch fails because its warrant hinges on an unverified physical premise. Whether the real physical arm, carrying its approach momentum and rotor inertia, actually achieves `{python} ReleaseWorkedVerdict.a_arm_str` within a fraction of a millimeter depends entirely on available joint torque, drive electromagnetic rise times, and structural joint stiffness. Because no empirical hardware trace in this book measures these dynamic properties under load, the premise remains *unknown*, and the entire claim branch must be refused.

The other branches fail the same way. The base's `{python} ReleaseWorkedVerdict.budget_str` partial budget excludes dispatch-to-admission delay and inherits illustrative values for credible deceleration, brake onset, tracking error, and localization, and its `{python} ReleaseWorkedVerdict.spare_str` spare is small against a plausible error in any one of them. The mug branch of C1 is refused on three premises. Its handover force sits under the criterion only for a free hand. The force comes from a standard's body model rather than a measurement of this contact, and nothing in this book shows that the handover geometry excludes the clamped case that would fail. Its grounding premise, that the object the arm grasps is the mug the task names, is unknown, because a confident grounding to a same-colored glass jar passes every geometric check (@sec-intent-request-to-proposal) and no record in this book settles which object the arm holds. The permission timing of C2 rests on a WCET declared at `{python} ReleaseWorkedVerdict.wcet_str` beside an unloaded `{python} ReleaseWorkedVerdict.enforcer_unloaded_str`, never measured under the placement's worst load. The `{python} ReleaseWorkedVerdict.t_age_str` dispatch age of C4 adds datasheet readout to illustrative pipeline terms. C5 and C6 cite records that this book describes but does not contain: the placement test ledger and a `PASS` record for each of A1–A4. C3 differs in kind. Its premise, floor friction of at least `{python} ReleaseWorkedVerdict.mu_min_str` on every aisle, can be surveyed on a dry floor, but a clear oil film looks like dry concrete to the cameras, and no measurement on the machine can exclude it.

Every claim therefore rests on at least one premise that the book's evidence leaves unknown, and the adjudicator signs `REFUSE`. The verdict does not find the machine unsafe. Its inputs are illustrative, so the decision is illustrative too. It shows how this release would be decided and cannot license the machine. Under the fourth law (@sec-boundary-bedrock-laws), a premise the evidence cannot settle must restrict operation, and on this evidence every claim carries one. The refusal names the measurements that would change it; a separately stipulated branch below completes that decision without treating those measurements as available. @Tbl-16-cond-measurements lists them, with the premise each settles and the restriction a supporting result would lift.

| Measurement                           | Premise it settles (value in this book)                                                                                                            | Claims | What a supporting result lifts                                                                                                                                                                |
|:--------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:-------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Stopping trials at the loaded mass    | Low-tail credible deceleration (`{python} ReleaseWorkedVerdict.a_brake_str`)                                                                       | C1     | The base's budget and its `{python} ReleaseWorkedVerdict.v_ceiling_str` ceiling, so an aisle speed can be signed                                                                              |
| Brake-onset trials                    | Brake onset (`{python} ReleaseWorkedVerdict.t_act_str`)                                                                                            | C1, C2 | The `{python} ReleaseWorkedVerdict.t_renewal_to_onset_str` bound from the last valid renewal to brake onset                                                                                   |
| End-to-end age trace                  | Dispatch age (`{python} ReleaseWorkedVerdict.t_age_str`) and subsequent evidence aging                                                             | C4     | The age term of the budget and the stale-data threshold                                                                                                                                       |
| Tracking-error and localization tails | Tracking bound (`{python} ReleaseWorkedVerdict.eps_track_str`) and localization bound (`{python} ReleaseWorkedVerdict.delta_loc_str`)              | C1     | The inset and overhead terms of the budget                                                                                                                                                    |
| Site survey                           | Rack-end clear distance (`{python} ReleaseWorkedVerdict.d_clear_str`)                                                                              | C1     | A signed speed at each surveyed rack end                                                                                                                                                      |
| Floor survey                          | Dry-floor friction (`{python} ReleaseWorkedVerdict.mu_dry_str`) against the `{python} ReleaseWorkedVerdict.mu_min_str` needed                      | C3     | Assessed route only, with maintained contamination exclusion and loaded stops at the qualified friction floor; reduced speed alone cannot exclude oil                                         |
| Inference trace                       | Chunk inference at the 99th percentile (`{python} ReleaseWorkedVerdict.t_chunk_str`)                                                               | None   | Service availability: characterize renewal within the `{python} ReleaseWorkedVerdict.t_lease_str` lease; a percentile does not guarantee each renewal, and C2 depends on independent fallback |
| Loaded enforcer timing                | Enforcer WCET (`{python} ReleaseWorkedVerdict.wcet_str`, declared)                                                                                 | C2, C5 | The `{python} ReleaseWorkedVerdict.deadline_str` deadline under the placement's worst load                                                                                                    |
| Arm stopping trials                   | Arm deceleration from the guarded approach (about `{python} ReleaseWorkedVerdict.a_arm_str` needed)                                                | C1     | Door opening at the guarded approach                                                                                                                                                          |
| Handover force trials                 | Peak contact force at the handover speed (`{python} ReleaseWorkedVerdict.f_handover_str` derived for a free hand) and absence of clamping geometry | C1     | Handing the mug to the coworker at `{python} ReleaseWorkedVerdict.v_handover_str` under `accept_item`                                                                                         |
